PEGGY : "I'd go to Brown's oftener to get my hair done, but you've to wait so long." Eliza: "Why don't you tell them to send it?' WILLING TO TAKE CHANCES.—First Tramp: "Do you think cigarettes is as injur'ous as they say?" Second Tramp: " Dunno, I wish I could get enough of dem to find out."

As THEY ALL Do.—" Of course, the bride's father gave her sway, but didn't anyone give away the groom?" "Oh, he gave himself away—asked her at\ their very first dinner at the hotel if she took cream and sugar in her coffee." MRS. SWELLINGTON : "Are you sure this is the fashion?" Modiste: "Yes, madame! Ze ver' latest." Mrs. Swellington : " Queer ! It looks well and feels comfortable."

"I MEANT to have told you of that hole," said a lady ton visitor, who had stumbled into a pit of water in her garden. "Never mind, madam, I found it out for myself !" SOME women believe so thoroughly that the way to a man's heart is throng his stomach that they give the man a bad case of indigestion trying to find it.

Alcibiades. finding his irregularities become the general topic of conversation at Athens, and having a very fine dog, which he had given a large sum of money for, he cut off his tail, which was reckoned a great ornament. His friends told him that the whole city blamed him for so foolish an action, and talked of nothing else. "That is what I meant,"oaid he, "I had rather that they should talk of my dog's tail than scrutinise my conduct." NATURE AND TEMPERANCE.—Temperance Man: My friend, what I want you to do is to throw your whisky bottle into the sea. Old Toper: I did that once, but the waves floated it back to me, and I Raid to myself if the laws of nature worked that way I wasn't to blame for takin' the bottle again, and—Temperance Man: Ah, but the bottle you threw away was empty. Throw it into the sea when the bottle is full of whisky, and you'll find the laws of nature are all right. Too NEAR HOME.—A Yorkshire socialist, ex. plainlng to a friend the principles of socialism, remarked that all possessions should be shared equally. "If you had two horse," said the friend, "would you give me one ?" "Of course," replied the socialist. " And, if you had two cows, would you do the same ?" "Of course I should." "Well, supposing now," said the friend, slowly, "you had two pigs, would you give me one of them ?" "Eli 1 tha's gettfn' ower near home," said the other, slyly; " tha knaws I've got two pigs."

NOTE HISTORICAL.—A remarkable statement once came to light in a Board school young lady's essay on "The Cruise of the Mayflower": "The Puritans found a lunatic asylum in the wilds of America." Subsequent investigation of this astounding allegation showed that the essayist had once learned that "the Puritans found an asylum in the wilds of America," and that she had added the adjective "lunatic" to give greater clearness to her narrative.

WHIRRAROO !—The following is told of one o- the heads of the family O'Moony who visited Lon- don not many years ago. Accustomed only to command, and being short oi funds, he entered the Bank of England and presented a cheque. Won- dering at the hesitation the clerk displayed in not at once giving him the "needful," he stated in strong and unhesitating terms that he was "The O'Moony of the Doon ' ; when, to his still greater @uprise, he was informed by the bank-clerk: "I don't care whether you are the O'Moony of the Doon, or the O'Doony of the Moon ! " " NEWMAN is a cycling novice, isn't he ?" asked Brown. "Novice? I should say he was IHe doesn't know a sprocket from a handle-bar," said Watkins. " Why, the other day we were plan- ning a ride for Saturday, and I told him to be sure and h-:ing his repair outfit. On Saturday, when ha came round to the house, I asked him if he had remembered the repair kit. 'Have I? he ex- claimed. Of course I have I'—and with these words he brought out a big leather pocket-book containing a box of salve, a small bottle of arnica, a roll of bandages, and about a square yard of court-plaster !" A HOUSEKEEPER tells this story: We had at one time in our employ a very green young woman. This young woman showed her intelligence on the first day of her service in our family. She was told to go out in the yard and take down the clothes- line, which was stretclud among half-a-dozen posits Bet up 19r thot tint-pose. She was at the job for so tong a time that we began to wonder what on earth was the matter with her. We went out to see what she was doing, and there we found her work- ing away vigorously with a spade. She had already dug up three of the posts, and had almost com- pleted the work on a fourth when we found her. She didn't stay with us long.

THERE are doctors and doctors ; among the most intelligent of all these friends of humanity was one who had the courage to give a bit of advice to the head of a family not many miles from New York. The head of the family was robust but exacting, healthy but irritable. "I don't know what is the matter with my family, doctor," he said; " but my wife is nervous, my children are suffering from something—l don't know what—in fact, the whole house is upset. Even the servants seem vacillating and bordering on nervous prostra- tion." "I think it would be all right," said the doctor, "if you took a six months' tour of Europe alone." "I, ' cried paterfamilias—" the only well member of the family 2" " Yes," said the doctor gravely; " you ought to travel for the health of your family. - - - - -

MR. FREDERIOK LOCKER-LAMPSON, in his "My Confidence," tells a story of an old sea-captain, a denizen of Greenwich Hospital in the old days. He had a faithful servant named John, who invariably provided a penny roll for his master's breakfast. One morning the breakfast-room bell rang, and John's master groaned, and said, in an agitated voice, "John, very ill. Go for Doctor Dobson. This is probably the beginning of my last illness." "Indeed, sir," said John, " I hope not. Whet is it, sir? What does you feel like?" "I am very bad indeed !" quoth his master. "I've entirly lost my appetite, John; I can't get through my penny roll !" " Eh," said John, much relieved; "when the baker came this mornin', all the penny rolls was gone, sir, so I gave you a twopenny one !" ACCOMMODATINGLY ACCOMMODATING.—An old gardener, on changing masters, found himself in the service of one of these wilful undecided men who retire from regular employment early and spend the remainer of their lite in restless unpro- fitable muddling. The hobby of the moment was arboriculture, and trees and shrubs were being planted one day and rooted up the next, arranged, disarranged, and rearranged, until the assistant, used to a more sympathetic manner with Nature, was well-nigh beside himself. Disuasion and argument being found to be alike inoperative with his master, he at length fell into a state of apathy, and restricted his conversation to two remarks. If the whim to move a tree and thus leave an open space seized the lord of the domain, and the gar- dener's advice was asked, he would reply, "Yes, sir—it will make a nice peep." Contrariwise, if it was decided to fill a space, he would reply, "Yes, sir—it will make a nice block." " Peep " and "block "—these were his two words. uttered without enthusiasm ; and he held to them until 'he planting craze was at an end. LAYING A GUOST. —ln his "Personal Recol- lections," Mr. C. K. Tuckerman tells a good story of the late Mr. Spurgeon. A lady whom the famous preacher was visiting had allotted to him a bedroom which was thought to be haunted. On the following morning she expressed great anxiety to hear how he had passed the night. The guest assured her that he had seldom slept better. "I am so glad !" remarked the lady. "Then you had no disturbances You received no—er— visitations ? The truth is I had to put you in the haunted chamber,' and I have been very nervous about it all night." " Well, madam, now you speak of its I did have a visitation," he replied. "About midnight i awoke, and discovered a veiled female stansling motionless by my bedside. As she seemed to have nothing particular to com- municate, I availed myself of the opportunity to appeal to her benevolence—a habit I have when in the presence of ladies; so, reaching under my pillow for a little book which I always carry about with me, I asked her to do me the favour to sub- scribe to my orphanage. Upon this she dis- appeared like a shot, and I never saw anything more of hr
THE MOST NUTRITiOUS.
(Copyright.) THE TEMPTATION OF DUNCAN RUTLAND.
BY JOSEPH HOCKING,
Author of "The Birthright," "Mistress Nancy Molesworth," "All Men are Liars," "The Story of Andrew Fairfax," &c.
CHAPTER XXVII. DUNCAN'S FIRST LOVE-LETTER.

At first Lady Neville could not believe her daughter's words. The confession was absurd, because, to her, it could not be true. "My child, you have taken leave of your senses," she said. "You are not well. My illness has been too much for you. We will go away from here, we will go back to England." "No, no, mother," cried the girl, "I am not ill, lam not speaking without thought. It is true, mother, it is true. I believed as long as I could; but—but I cannot believe longer." Lady Neville was no longer able to control her feelings. Her daughter's words entirely unnerved her; for a moment she was overcome by her confession. .

—C`Tnithis is your work, I suppose," she cried, bitterly, turning to Rutland, "this is your idea of honour. Not content with disturbing our town with your pernicious doctrines, you seek to pour poison into my child's mind. This is baseness personified." Alizon sprung to her feet before Rutland could reply. Her mother's words made her feel sensitive to the pain she had given her. "It is false, nother," she replied. "Duncan has never uttered one word to persuade me to change my faith. Never breathed a wish, in my hearing, that I should cease to be a Catholic." "Then why this madness, why this treason to the faith which not only the Nevilles, but the Bartons, have held for hundreds of years ? " "I cannot give you many reasons, mother, except that I find it impossible to believe. Until that discussion I believed without question. I had been taught to regard all non-Catholics as heretics, and I never for a moment doubted the absolute truth of all the claims of the Church. Even when Father Sheen failed to deal with the difficulties which Duncan raised at the discussion, 1 did not doubt. I felt sure that everything was right, although I could not understand. I did not feel a bit influenced by what he said in his speeches, although he seemed certain of the things he spoke about. As you know, mother, it was your wish that he should be converted, and--" "This has nothing to do with your madness," cried Lady Neville, interrupting her. For the first time she realised that she had been guilty of trying to do that for which she censured Rutland in such unmeasured terms. "This has nothing to do with your madness," she repeated, angrily. "What makes you give up your salvation and become the child of lies ? " _ _ _

"I have not given up salvation," replied the girl, "rather I have realised it. I have come to see that it is not to be obtained by penances and confessions and repeating prayers, and--" "Silence!" cried her ladyship, sternly. "I will not have you utter such blasphemy. Who taught you to say these things? What led you to this heresy? " "I could not help it, mother, I really could not," replied the girl. "What really opened my eyes, and led me to doubt was—that Bambino, to which your restoration to health has been attributed." _ _ _ _
"That is only a venerated relic, child," said her ladyship. "Belief in its power has not become an article of faith."

"But it has been venerated by the Church, it has been declared to have miraculous power, and this by the Pope's consent. The priest attributed your recovery to its influence." "Well, and why not ? " "Because there was not a shadow of evidence. It had no more to do with your recovery than any doll I might buy in a shop!" cried the girl. • "Well, and what then Suppose it had not, surely there was not enough in such a trifling incident to lead you:to change your faith." "Not in !Fself. But it led me to consider other things. It. led me to examine the evidences on which the doctrines were built, and I saw that in many cases they were mere legend, mere fable, bolstered up by the authority of the Church." "and where had you the opportunity of examining evidences, you foolish child." "I found a New Testament, I read it through, and I found that many of the doctrines in which I believed had no foundation there, and oh, com- pared with the teaching of Christ, that of the Church seemed so poor, so trivial." "How dare you I How can you, an ignorant girl, understand these things? Besides, the Church has expressly forbidden you to judge of such matters." 'And why should I not ? ' asked Alizon. "I have my life to live, and God has given me some intelligence; besides, I have prayed many hours, and God has opened my eyes. I cannot help it, mother, neither can I altogether explain how it came to be; but many of my old beliefs left me, just as my belief in the story of Cinderella left me. In some things I still believe. The doctrines which are common to all Christians are real, but those on which the Papacy rests are to me unbelievable. • I cannot, cannot acccept them. Why, this Rome, this Mecca of the Church, is the very home of supersti- tion, of baseless legend, of Pagan relics. Why, even the ceremony we saw to-day has no suggestion of the Christianity of the New Testament. Oh, I held on as long as I could, I struggled and prayed to keep on believing, but I could not, mother, I could not!" _

The girl's overtaxed nerves gave way, 'and she burst into passionate sobs, while Lady Neville stood by in speechless anger. , "Mr. Rutland, I wish to be alone with my daughter," she said presently. "When you are gone, I shall doubtless be able to bring her to reason." _

"Of course, I will go since you bid me," said Rutland. "But, but--" "I have given you my answer; it is impossible, it is madness. You will be wise, you will be kind to both Alizon and me, if you adhere to your former resolution, and go to Naples to-morrow." "No," said Rutland, "I shall not go." "And why, pray ? " "Because Alizon claims my protection." -- "Your protection. Against whom, pray " "Against you and those you will select as your advisers," replied Rutland, quietly. "I think I told you I desired Co be left alone," said her ladyship presently. "It is not for me to answer you." "Then I must go." He took a step towards Alizon. _ _

"I forbid you to go near my daughter," said her ladyship. "Kindly go." "Thank you, your ladyship. Good-night, Alizon. Remember I shall always try to be near you, and that I shall be always loving you." He left the room, leaving mother and daughter together. The next morning when Rutland went into the breakfast-room of the hotel, he looked everywhere for Lady Neville and Alizon, but they were nowhere to be seen.

Utilising his small knowledge of Italian, he asked a servant for information. The only answer he was able to obtain was that the Countess had vacated the apartments. The woman knew nothing else, however, and as Rutland had a difficulty in under- standing her, he made his way to the entrance hall. The concierge spoke English fairly fluently, as indeed, he seemed to speak all other languages. Yes, the lady, whom he persisted in calling "the Countess," left the hotel that morning. "At what time did she go ? " asked Rutland. "Soon after eight o'clock." "Where did she go? Have they left Rome ? " "I do not know where they are gone; except that they have left Rome." "But she left instructions concerning her letters? " "Certainly." "She gave you an address to which you should forward them?"

"Certainly." "What is the address?" "I am sorry to disappoint you, signore, but you must please excuse me," said the Italian. "They are gone back to England," he concluded at len&th. "Lady Neville has taken Alizon home that es may get the advice of Ritzoom and Sheen." But he had no sufficient reason for believing in this, as he knew that Lady Neville was not sufficiently strong to bear continuous travelling. He felt he could not stay longer in Rome. Now that Alizon had gone, the city had lost its charm. "Yes, that is it," he said at length. "Alizon has gone to England, and I will go too. I will catch the midnight train to-night, and return as fast as I can; I shall then be near to help her." Ho walked into the Piezza del Polo. then slops

The Wrecked Indra.--Safety .of the Crew.

The missing crew uf the British steamer lndra, from Mauritius, which was wrecked on August 20th, 22 miles south of Cape Guardafui, have been landed on the Arabian Coast near Makalla. A local steamer has been despatched to bring the men to Aden. It will be remembered that one of the crew is Mr. Eric Joynson, a native of Warrington. Death of Mrs. Dale.

After a long and painful illness Mrs M. J. Dale, wife of Mr. R. Dale, 59, Sankey-street. Warrington' died on September 4th. The late Mrs. Dale had been a member of the Methodist Church for more than forty years, and touching references were made to the loss the Church has suffered by her departure at both services in Bold-street Chapel last Sunday. At the evening service the preacher, the nev.C. H. Ilocken, read a short statement giving an account of her conversion and of her earnest and useful Chritian life. She bore her sufferings with wonderful resignation and passed away in great peace. The service concludei by the singing of the hymn, "Give me the wings of faith to rise within the veil, and see."

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
MY DEAR NELLIE,

It seems that the milliners this year 4re harking back to handkerchief toques, which they make in very bewitching forms of plaited taffetas threaded through with eagle quills and little grouse wings. There is also to arrive among us that most graceful and feminine of hats a black chip shape with a rather tall crown, the big drum bent down- wards in front and the back, and all the trimming the hat can boast is a couple of long scarlet ostrich plumes, starting in front from the anchorage of a velvet-coloured buckle. Strings of black or scarlet velvet are becoming adjuncts of such a piece of headgear, and if fastened jauntily beneath the left ear are piquant in their effect. In some quarters broad-brimmed, flat-crowned hats are quite pre- dominant, often laden with lovely, full-blown roses. On some models, an attempt is made to keep pace with the flying days by substituting such autumn flowers as sunflowers, hollyhocks, and dahlias, but with the exception of the last, which are singularly successfully imitated, they are not greeted with much enthusiasm.

The Eton coat will be worn as much as ever this autumn and winter. Most of the new furs take this shape. It is a very sensible one, for it is only in the very coldest of weather that we need an outer layer of fur over the warm winter dress round the hips. The back and chest are the portions of cold. The arms are well shielded with long fur sleeves that come down in points over the hands. A few of the fur sleeves open slightly out in bell. shape at the wrists. Many will prefer this shape, which makes it very easy to slip into the coat. When the sleeves are closely fitting the whole way down, the indolence natural to human nature dis- inclines one to get into the coat, and a draught- encouraging cape is picked up and donned instead. The proper penalty arrives pretty punctually. Cloth coats for autumn wear are scarcely different from those of last year, except in the modified character of the sleeves, which are wider at the wrist than above it. The three-quarter length coat is again to have a trial, and may possibly suc- ceed in favourably impressing the public.

The ordinary morning shirt consists of two fronts, either plain or set with minute tucks at the shoulder seam, with a box pleat down the centre. This box pleat is formed of a double fold of material, machine stitched at the edge, and put on separately over the edge of the right front; into this the buttonholes are worked. Many shirts have been made this year with what is termed the saddle yoke, a shaped piece in front coming from the shoulder seam, like that at the back. It gives additional strength and a smarter look than when the fulness is all congregated into the seam and collar band. More and more as the season advances do we behold the increasing use of rib- bons of all sorts as an ornament to dress. Golden gauze ribbons are very much used, and silver thread is woven into many backgrounds. The brocaded and fancy ribbons are more fashionable than the plain kinds.

No one can tell how soon the bad weather may return, and it is well to order_ a smart autumn costume in good time. A very becoming one, just completed, is made of khaki serge. The skirt is unlined and untrimmed, save for a few rows of machine stitching up each seam, and round the hem. It fastens at one side of the front, where a useful little pocket is slipped in, just large enough to hold one of the small handkerchiefs of the moment. The bodice is of the jacket order, and has a very short basque at the back, gradually lengthening towards the fronts, where it dips downwards in a kind of rounded tab at either side. There is a deep, flat collar of the serge itself, closely covered with narrow rows of gold and silver braid, placed alternately. The sleeves, where they widen out towards the wrists, are lined with braid to match the collar, a single row show- ing at the edge on the upper side. The fronts of the little coat do not quite meet, but show a vest of chiffon in a lovely tone of blue, like that of a sunset sky above the rosy clouds. The high collar is in white embroidery, with a bow of the same at the neck. _ _

I have often been impressed with the fact that too many of us wear gaudy petticoats in doubtful weather. Whenever it is to be managed without extravagance, it is well to have the petticoat match the dress in colour. A nut-brown cloth dress, made for travelling wear, has a petticoat of nut-brown moirette to match it. This latter is far from being a costly item, being bought ready made for a sum which gives a nice little handful of silver in change for a sovereign. Moirette wears well;. far better than silk. The brown cloth dress in question is made with a pleated skirt, a row of narrow black guipure outlining each pleat. The Eton coat has long fronts, but reaches only to the waist at the back. It is bordered with the black guipure, and has revers of pastel-blue cloth, dotted with black. The front is made of cream-coloured net, embroidered in pastel- blue, mauve, and pink, and drawn down in folds over the palest possible sky-blue silk. Your loving JENNIE.

In the event of the Queen going to Germany next month, on a visit to the Empress Frederick, Her Majesty will travel direct from Scotland, probably via Harwich , and the Hook of Holland, returning to Windsor about the middle of November. The health of the Empress Frederick is causing much anxiety to the Royal Family, and unless a change for the better takes place, tha Queen is understood to have decided to go to Germany to see her eldest daughter. Her Majesty would go first to , Friedrichshof, afterwards proceeding to Coburg. The Queen has stayed many times at Darmstadt, but she has never been more than once or twice to Coburg. Dalrneny. where the coming of age festivities in con- nection with Lady Sibyl Primrose are in full swing, has never been a show place. The present house, which Lord Rosebery has enlarged, is modern, and the gardens are not remarkable • the woods however are fine, and there are many grand old trees. Lady Sybyl though unquestionably the prettier of the sisters, is not perhaps se bright and sparkling as Lady Crewe,hut her manners are charming, and she is immensely popular. When quite tiny, she won temporary celebrity by composing and despatching a letter to the Queen which began—as she explained afterwards—with "Your Majesty," and ended "From your loving Sibyl." The Queen has always taken the warmest interest in Lord Rosebery's motherless daughters, and has, upon more than one occasion, been heard to remark that they are" just what girls ought to be." Lady Sibyl has been staying at Schwalbach lately, taking the cure. The town of Schwalbach is beautifully situated at one end of a valley, and surrounded by pictureeque dark pine woods, with charming walks and drives, all round. There are two springs where people go quite early in the day, to drink the waters, while the mud baths—the chief feature of the Schwaltach cure are taken as a rule about ten o'clock in the morning. There is a beautiful casino in the town where dances take place, and a big cbocolate shop,wbere everyone congregates in the after- noon to drink, and—gossip. The National Union of Women Workers will hold its , annual Conference at Brighton next month, under the presidency of the Hon. Mrs. Lyttlelton, wife of the Bishop of Southampton. Many interesting aubjecEr will be discussed by orators whose opinions will carry weight including Lady Aberdeen, Lady Battersea, Mrs. Henry Fawcett, Mrs. Humphry Ward, Mrs Creighton, and others. There will be discourses upon the modern home, the housing problem, domestic service, foreign missions, the management of the household, and so on. A new feature on this occasion will be the appearance of Mr. Whittaker, M.P., and Dr. Branthwaite, who will discuss the subjects of Inebriate Homes and temperance Legis- latien. Hitherto the Conferences have been confined to ' women speakers, though there was a mixed platform at the International Congress of women last year. One of the principal firms of house agents in London, recently suggested a new occupation for women, by applying for certificates for a number of female bailiffs, or in other words, officers of the court, who are put in possession when a distraint is levied upon a person's geode and chattels. No doubt there are cases in which such an arrangement would be appropriate, and some people would perhaps cheerfully surrender their goodsto a pretty and entortaisting "hbailiffess." Butat the same time, one can hardly imagine that the profession would be a pleasant one to follow. The idea is, of course, that a woman would do better where the person levied upon is of: the same sex, but, as a rule, the case of people who are subject to these harsh measures of the law, are not the most refined, and in these cases, the alteration would doubtless lead to an increase of asperities rather than tend to make things pleasanter. Severely practical people will doubtless ask of what possible use such a feat could provc, but however, this may be, the fact remains that Madame Von Isacescu acted very pluckily in her attempt to swim from Calais to Dover. Probably if any woman could have succeeded she would have done so, but at least Madame Von Isacescu has given us another illustration of the sustain- ing power of sugar, which already had been remarked in South Africa. It will, moreover, be noted that, true to the traditions of our sex,the brave swimmer depended largely upon tea, as a stimulant to her much-taxed energies. Although the causes are probably accidental, yet it is interesting to note that during the summer months a very large number of visitors from the continent have been seen in these; islands. It is the rule for many Americans to visit Britain during the summer, whether on the way to or from Paris, or, in order to spend the whole of their holiday hare, but this year there has ?men in addition a large inflow of French and German visitors From Scotland it is reported that the number of French and German tourists has been quite exceptional, and many people who are staying at the Tarr English and Welsh seaside rEsorts, state that they find there a large proportion of foreigners. The gold element is seldom missing from up-to-date tailor-made gowns. This takes the form of embroidery braiding, or perchance buttons, the same touch being repeated in the headgear supplied with such toilettes. On black.dark brown, dark blue and dark gteen,a touch of gold is decidedly fascinating, but great care should be tat.:Kt int to overdo it, as in such a case the result must be vulgar. When laboriously buttonholing hooks and eyes, with silk to match the color of the garment on which they are being sewn, it must frequently have eccured to us how delightful it would be it these useful little items were to appear on the market in other eracles than the universal black and white. In this direction however, our troubles may, at length be said to be over. The happy mom- eat has arrived when it is possible to obtain enamelled hooks and eyes in all fashionable shades. Still further I therefore, has the home dressmaker had her path smoothed for her. .

Evening coiffures grow more and more ela,horate, as regards decoration. Last year, a twist of tulle, a light osprey, or a flower only. was in evidrrce, but at the present time quite formidable erections of featheri, flowers. tulle, chiffon, lace, rtn.. are to be seen at all fashionable assemblies. BURT flowers of some brilliant hue, arranged behind the left ear, are much patroniFed by girls, a mode for which the" Geisha" is undoubt- edly respcnsible. One can scarcely credit the statement that the house- fly can bite, the results of which a child is certified to have died, in one of the London Hospitals recently. It is customary to speak of a mosquito bite, but even that vicious little insect ices not employ any such violent methods. It pierces the skin, with its delicate spear- like instruments, but the house-fly can neither bit 3 nor pierce, though it can without doubt convey poissumus infection, and which, in this case, resulted in the death of the child.

At the inquest, the Medical Officer of Health said, that too little attention was paid to the prominent part played by the common house fly in spreading disease. It is however difficult to know what cats be done, be yond keeping food and eatables as much from them as possible. Perhaps if everyone was to wage war upon the house fly in summertime, some little impression might be made in reducing their number, though even this is doubtful, and one might almnst as well try to count the stars in the heavens, so impossible would it seem to exterminate the little pests. However welcome a draught from the waters of Lethe may be to some folks, there are nevertheless few who would welcome the pretaste of its effects which Admiral Close states is to be found in Switz-rland. It cannot, ho says, be ten generally known that there is a spirit made in Switzerland from the mountain ash berry and sold in some of the Alpine Hotels, which has the power of destroying the memory. If that is so, it is to be hoped that steps will be taken very speedily by the Swiss Government to prohibit the sale of this stuff which, if its effect is as stated, is one of the most dan— gerous of poisons. " MADGE."

the uorso, and presently returned by way or the Via dei Condotti. When he reached the hotel, he realised that he was not strong enough to take the journey to England. The experiences of the last twenty-four hours revealed to him the fact that he had not yet recovered his strength. He was sick and faint. He went to his room and threw himself on hie bed. For a time he thought he was going to faint; but presently he recovered himself. Th. first dinner-bell rang, and he rose and dressed. "I think I will try and go after all," he said presently. "I feel much stronger now; besides, I want to be on the move. I cannot stay in Rome now Alizon is gone." When he reached the smoking-room, he saw men reading letters. Evidently the evening post had come. He did not expect any himsilf, but he mechanically made his way to the entrance hall, where the letter-rack was placed. Turning to the space containing the number of his room, he saw that several had arrived for him. He scanned them eagerly in the hope that Alizon had been able to send him a line, but he saw at a glance that they were all from England. "I will not read them until after dinner," she thought, as the second dinner-bell rang. "Perhaps they will help to distract my mind." When dinner was over, he found his way into the billiard-room, which was quite deserted. There was only ;we letter of importance, and that was from Tudor Church secretary. It contained the news that the pulpit had been supplied for four Sundays more, and while the church longed for his return, the church officers had forwarded his next quarter's salary, with a resolution, unanimously passed, that he must not come back until he was perfectly restored to health. The letter decided him. "No, I'll not go back yet," he said; "besides, Alizon may to in Italy. I'll follow Lady Neville's advice, and go to Naples. I promised myself that I would see Pompeii and Vesuvius before returning to England." By two o'clock the next day he had reached the capital of Neapolia, and was, from his hotel windows, looking at the finest bay in the world. At the end of four days, however, he wanted to be on the move again. His mind was racked with anxiety about Alizon ; he fanci(d all sorts of gloomy pictures, and called to mind what Catholic girls had often had to suffer when they doubted the faith of their fathers. On the morning of the fifth day in Naples. how- ever, a letter was brought to his room which made all things new. It was a letter from Alizon which had been forwarded from Rome. It was the first letter he had ever received from her, and he broke the seal with all the eagerness of a boy of fifteen. "I have a great difficulty in writing you, Duncan," she said, "for everyone seems against me, even my maid. But still, Ido not mind, I am very happy, happier than I ever hoped to be in this life; perhaps it is because I still have hope of a greater happiness in the future. As you will know ere this, we left Rome suddenly; my mother willed that we should, and I thought it best not to refuse to accompany her. She is far from strong, and my action has hurt her more than you can think. We shall not stay here long. Where we shall go Ido not know, but probably to Venice. You can guess the reason why I am kept in ignorance. It seems very strange that mother and I, who have been such friends, should be opposed to each other; but I cannot help it. lam trying to be kind and patient and cheerful, although it is difficult to do so. Mother thinks it wise to taunt me because I have ceased to be a Catholic, and to accuse me of being a traitor to the truth. It is what I should have done under similar circumstances a few months ago, so I must not complain. She also continues to be angry because of you, but 1 brave that anger gladly, for through you, life is more glorious than I had ever conceived that it could be. "Mbther will, ram sure, never consent for us to be more to each other than we are now; but even if we are not I shall continue to rejoice.

"I think of you continually. Tale care of your- self, Duncan, my beloved. Do not be anxious about me, nor let yourself be unhappy, for your happi- ness is more to me than my own. I wish I could ask you to write, but I cannot, neither must you expect another letter from me, for I am afraid I shall not have another opportunity of writing. "Mother is surrounding me with priests, learned and grave, in the hopes of leading me back to her faith; she is also trying to make me believe that my love for you is madness. But she fails in both these things—fails because I know in whom I have believed '—fails, because my love for you grows stronger each hour. Be sure of this, Duncan, whatever happens." That same day Duncan started for Florence, where he stayed for two or three days; and after making sure that Alizon had left that city, he took train for Venice. His mind was full of anxious thoughts; but as he read and re-read Alizon's letter, he could not help rejoicing with great joy.

"Well, what is the meaning of this, Sheen? " It was Father Ritzoom who spoke, and the old parish priest noticed that the Jesuit was boa; anxious and angry. They were sitting together irc the study of the former in Lynford, and both were burning the fragrant weed. "You know as much as I do now," replied Father Sheen. "Lady Neville sent for me as soon as she arrived, the day before yesterday, and on hearing her news, I immediately telegraphed for you." "I've been a fool," said Ritzoom presently. "Most wise men become fools sometimes," replied Father Sheen. _ _
"But my foolishness is inexcusable. If I were a boy just completing his novitiate, I could not have muddled the business more."

"I thought it a splendid plan." "So it was, but I reckoned wrongly. I forgot that women live outside the realm of any known law, and I did not realise that Rutland's prejudices were so deeply-rooted." "Of course, it was my fault in the first instance," said Father Sheen, ruefully ; "but for my giving that series of addresses all this would never have happened." "There's no knowing," said Ritzoom. "No, of course that is so, and really, when I understood your plans, I thought that *Providence had interfered, and would overrule everything for the glory of the Church." Ritzoom sat quietly for. several minutes, his face looking more like a mask than the features of a living man. "Did you see Alizon ? " asked Ritzoom presently. "Oh, yes."

" "Oh, she was very kind to me, but I saw that all my authority had gone." "You never had much, I am afraid." "Well, there was always an atmosphere of liberty in the house, but I never knew a time when she would disobey me in matters of religion." "Did you say anything to her about Rutland?" "No. I—l—, somehow I dared not."
"And did you speak to her about her change of faith? "

"No, I did not think it best then." Ritzoom laughed quietly. He read this simple- minded priest's thoughts like a book. "You were wise." "What are you going to do?" asked Father Sheen, after several minutes' silence. "I am trying to think. Give me another cigar!" The Jesuit smoked for several minutes in perfect stillness. His face was utterly expressionless, his eyes were 6c:dui. "Well ?" sa:d Sheen preseniy. "It's nor, well, it's baci." _ _ _

"Yes, it is bad. I see no loophole anywhere.- Even although her ladyship persists in her refusal--" "Which she will." "Yes ; well, even if Alizon disobeys her mother--" "Which she will not." "I don't know."
"I believe von." "Well. coti'le•now, what do you suggest? Let's face the facts." __

"That's what I've been doing ever since I entered this beastly town." There could be no doubt about it, Ritzoom was very angry. His impatient, curt replies to his friend, the rasping tone of his voice revealed the fact completely. "Sheen, as you know, I've been engaged on delicate matters for more than twenty years. During that time I've failed only twice to carry out my plans." "I am surprised at your failing at all," replied Father Sheen.

"My first failure was when I was a very young man. I need not give you the details of the affair. But I failed utterly. I was altogether inexperienced at the time, so I may be excused. For twenty years after that, everything I touched succeeded. I was very careful, and I never attempted the impossible. Then I bungled another matter." "Indeed!" "Yes. I matched my wits with a fellow by the name of Lancaster. In some things I outmost I
neat rum, but in others I—well, I came off second best. That was so long ago; and I made a vow that I would never be beaten again." "Ahl"

"i-o-ti may zuess, therefore, how I feel about this business. It is more serious than you cam think." "I am afraid it is all my fault," sighed the old' priest. "Pah 1 it was no longer your fault when I took the matter up. I promised that I would turn your failure into a victory for the Church, and instead, unless strong, definite action is taken, it will meats just the opposite. Not only has the Protestant remained a Protestant, but the girl will give LIP her faith, if the man is allowed to. influence her. "She has given up her faith!: suggested Sheen. " N onsense. " "But, but--"

"My dear man, the faith is not given up so' easily, it is woven into every fibre of her being, she is the child of many generations of Catholics. She still belongs to us." "But her mother told me that-"

"Oh, yes, yes, I understand. I've made a mess - of it, but lam not quite in my dotage. She is & woman, and she is a young woman. She has bees brought. up in an atmosphere of spiritual authority. Her mother remains true and exercises control; therefore she cannot cease to believe so easily. far as she is concerned it is only a matter of carer. ful, skilful management."

Father Sheen lOoked doubtful. "It is the man about whom I am most troubled. We have no hold upon him. I made un my mind that he should be converted, I promised you that he should be, and—and, well, I'd move heaver' and earth rather than be beaten."

"I don't think you understand Alizon." "No." "I don't. lam afraid—oh, I am—l'm not sure- that Alizon will not—not marry Rutland." Ritzoom took no notice of the other's words; evidently he regarded them as unworthy of all answer.
"Well, what are you going to do ? " asked the old priest rather testily. "I am going to have a conversation with Alizon." . . . "Yes and then ? " shall s;all call on Rutland."
"He is not in England." "But he soon will be. He'll find out where the girl is, and then--" Ritzoom shrugged hie' shoulders.

"Well, suppose you fail with them ? " "I shall not fail, at any rate with Alizon." "But suppose you do?" "Well, then, my friend," and Ritzoom's eye., flashed dangerously, "if that happens you will see some-" But he did not conplete the sentence. "When are you goinc, to see Alizon ?" The Jesuit looked at his watch. "To-night," he answered, like a man who had made up his mind to undertake a difficult task. "Then we must start at once." "Yes, at once." "Shall I call a cab ? " "No, we will walk. And I have a request to make of you." "What is that?" "Do not speak to me as we walk to the Priori unless I speak to you first." The two men started on their journey. After they had walked a few minutes Ritzocm stopped. " Did I not toll you ? " he said. They were standing opposite Tudor Chapel, which loomed large in the dim light, and cast dark shadow on the street. " What ? " asked Sheen. Rutland's church."
"I see nothing ha

"Don't you see that announcement ? " Leaning against one of the huge pillars which supported the portico was a notice-board, on which an announcement was made. The old priest put on his spectacles and read it. "A welcome home meeting next Saturday night," he said. "Evidently his church officers know' when they may expect him." Ritzoom did not reply, but walked quietly on. No other word was spoken until they reached the door of the Priory. Father Sheer, had obeyed hie orders. Lady Neville received the two men with cordiality, but there was an anxious look in her eyes. she said. "Thank you for coming so promptly As 1U"I want a quiet chat with you very much. may imagine, I am sorely troubled." .."Yes,' replied Ritzoom, "we had better have ' private interview at once." oat He uttered the word "private' with 6to emphasis that Father _Sheen expressed a desire

go into the library and read the Times. tbst "Will you give me a detailed account of all happened in Rome?" said the Jesuit, when the two were seated in Lady Neville's private eittill; room. "Please omit nothing. The merest tri may be of importance." "I will tell you all I can remember," replied Lady Neville, and forthwith she described faith' fully what had happened. "We had a terrible scene after Rutland left eel that night, simply terrible. / could not be" believed that she could have conceived such terrible heresy. She said that Romanism was not religion at all, and that its teaching was entirely wanting in the essentials of Christianity." Ritzoom looked very grave. "She still obeys you ? " he queried presentlP) "Yes," replied her ladyship, doubtfully. The priest understood perfectly the 'affirmative answer, as well as the tone in which it was spokee_:i "What are you prepared to sacrifice?" he die' presently. "Anything, everything." "That is well." "You would not consent to her manila Rutland?" "I would rather see her dead." "That is well," repeated the priest, with a sati....r fled smile. "Do you think she would disobey Ye' direct commands?" "No, I think not. She has always been a goeci,_ girl, and in spite of her apostacy, I am sure eel" loves me as much as ever." "Do not call it apostacy, Lady Neville. not regard it in that light. Most children 115_,,fe childish complaints, but we do not think of Ow; seriously; they get over them. Let us say ths" your daughter has an attack of spiritual meager' I do not think the attack is serious, and I cl° assure you she will get over it." "You have not seen her, Father Ritzoom; 9° have not spoken to her since she came froei Rome." "No, but Ido not think it matters. I fano,' understand the situation." * Lady Neville looked at the Jesuit keenly. For moment she doubted his powers. His very Olt deuce, while cheering her, made her afraid that did not understand her daughter's disposition character. Moreover, she could not be remembering that it was through Ritzoom wrft, Duncan and Alizon had been thrown together. was at his instigation that they had visited Re e; rather than some other Continental city. "ilt a the present nothing that he had prophesied come to pass, rather events had taken place vie.' threatened to darken the rest of her life. "What do you intend to do? "she asked presentlr "I cannot tell you exactly until I have beu!! interview with your daughter," replied Ritzni "But you need not be afraipl. Your daughter sola soon be ashamed of her/fancy for Rutland, all she will bitterly repent her momentary doubts." "I um very glad you think so," replied fled Neville. "I should like to see her at once," said Ritz 015 "the sooner we take action the better." ._,„„ 0, "Very well, I will send for her immedier,w' And she rung for a servant. (To be continued.)

div.head: FATALITY AT THE CABLE WORKS.
div.p: THE FATALITY AT THE CABLE WORKS.
An Unprotected Shaft.
The Company Heavily Fined,

A ease of much local interest vas heard at the War- Tin:4,ton Police Court cn Friday, whec, charges under the Factory and Workshops Act of 1878 were preferred against the St. Helens and Warrington Electric Cable 'Co., Limited. In the first irs!ance the firm was sum- moned tor failing to fence certain machinery, whereby 'Elizabeth Allen,was killed on July sth.The Company was also charged with having on the third of June employed a woman named Mary Clarke, that day being Sunday, and thore were similar chares for the same date in respect to Susan Clarke, Matilda Davies, Annie Oultram, Mary Ellen Kelly, Annie Price, May Stewart, and Maggie Whitfield —Major Roe, the District Factory Inspec!or, conducted the prosecution, and the defendant Company was renre. sented by Mr %V HS Oulton (Oppenheim and Malkin, St. Helens), who pleaded guilty to the charges. Mr Crompton was present on behalf of the relatives of the 'deceased girl. In opening the case, Major Roe said the offences with which the defendants were charged were of a very serious nature, and he was sorry to say that the young woman who W9B killed there met with her death through an unfenced shaft which was only ten inches above the ground and projected 59r1113 eighteen inches beyond the

table on which tEie machines, which the shift was driving rested. There were at least eighteen inches of this naked shaft —which was about an inch and a half or two inches in diameter—exposed, and it had been so running, coupled up to the original shafting for two or three days. A large number of women and young Persons were employed in the room and the shaft was in such a position that anyone passing might have their clothing caught in it, and would be dashed to pieces tong before the engine could be stopped. Major Ra, proceeded to quote section sof the original Act of 1878 amended by section 6 of 1891 which provided for the fencing of machinery and making the occupier liable to a fine not exceeding £lOO. Continuing he informed the Bench that the factory occupied by the defendants was visited by his colleague on the 29th of December last and the managing director was told that he must fence this particular shafting as it; was dangerous and a notice in writing was sent to the firm shortly after that ' date. No notice was taken of this and the shafting dwas running from the 19th of December to the data of this fatal accident, although the particular part of shafting that killed the young weman had been coup ed up to the original and fenced. shafting only a few days before. With refer- ence to the other offence, eight women were employed on Sunday. Not only was Sunday woik absolutely forbidden for women but the Factory Act limited the hours of work in such a factory to sixty hours per week. He had investigated the matter and found that some of the young women had workac.l 81A hours. le mentioned this to show that the young women were being exces- sively worked. Mr. Oulton in answer to questions by the Mayor atated that this particular machinery was not in ex• istence at the time of the Inspector's visit and they had not had notice regarding the fencing of it. The Mayor (to Major Roe) : I understood you to say that the particular shafting which caused the death of the unfortunate girl had been running from the 29th of December to July sth unfenced. It would now appear if the evidence is correct that it was an additional ph ce of shafting put on only a few days before July sth and this portion only was unfenced. Major Roe: I think I shall have to call some of my witnes,es as to that. I was not in the factory the whole of the time and could not have been expected to be. I do not know bow many days the shaft was Zunnine.

The Mayor: What I have in mind is this. It aggra- vates the nature of the offence very materially if the statement is correct that the particular shafting which caused the death of the girl bad been left unfenced from the 29th of December to the date of the accident. If,on the other hand the main body of tha shafting to which You called attention on December 29th was fenced in and this portion was an addition which had only been running for two or three days, it is rather a difference. Major Roc : My evidence is clear. I visited the place immediately after the adjourned inquest, and I then found that not only was thls extra length unfenced but two small tables with small saafting underneath Which my cllleague,Mr Smith, had ordered to be fenced, Were still unfenced. I have E'en it fenced since.

Maiir Roe wag then swozn and gave evidence. He Said that on the 7th of July be visited the factory and found that the whole of the shafting in the braiding ?Gem was unfenced. He ordered it to be fenced imme- diately and it had been fenced since. The Mayor: Do you say that on the 7th Ju)y, two lays after tho accident that you found the whole of the Shafting in the room unfenced ? Major Roe: The whole of it with the exception of a few drums which were put up here and there to take off the wire. These were not fencPs at all. Mr. Chilton: We are only concerned to-day with the 'able which has the projecting shaft. ho you say there were prpjecting shafts to more tables than one ?—I did 3ot say
Theis is one table with a projecting shaft P Certahily. _ _
You tell the I3cmch that table was in existence on the 29th of December ?—I do not.

You said you gave notice on the 29th of December for Um fencing of the projecting shaft. —No I did not. Are you aware that on the receipt of the notice the Company spent £3OO in carrying out your instructions: I am not aware. If I put that as a fact you will not dispu'e it could not dispute it. The Mayor said the only evidence they had was to the offect that the premises were visited on the 29th of December, and notice was given verbally that the shaft- was not fenced. That notice was followed by one to the same effect a few days later and the only evidence before the court was that the shaft remained unfenced until the accident.

Mr. Oulton :That was Hot the shafting that caused the aecdent. The Mayor: Wh;t is before tho Court 13 that there has been an utter disregard of the recommendations of the Inspector. Mr. Oulton : We are not summoned for that.

The Mayor: The fact in urged that the whole of the 'waft was unfenced; not only the particular piece that caused the death of the girl. Inspector Smith was then called and stated that he visited the factory on the 29th of December. The factor, was a new one, and had only been occupied 'some eight weeks. He found in the braiding room a long table on which were machines and underneath there was some low shafting. Ho pointed nut to the Managing director that the shaft was highly dangerous. He disputed the statement and pointxl out that it was Partially protected by drums on which the insulated "ire was wrapped. Witness told him that the shafting Must be protected so that no person could approach it on any pretext whatever. He confirmed the instructions by writing three days after his visit. He had not been to the works since.

Mary Ellen Kelly,the forewoman in the braiding room Raid Bho entered the erllllo.l Of the firm in January, and ,bad }seen engaged as forewoman for two months. She knew the table under which the shaft by which Allen Iras killed, was at work. The shaft was not running on the Monday previous to the accident and she thought It had only been running one day when the woman was Itilled. She did not know when t4e shaft was added to the old one.

Another employee named Nellie Stewart was called but fitle did not know when the extra piece of shafting was coupled up. She had never noticed it. The table had only been in use about three weeks. Councillor Plerpoint : The girls 'working in the room Must have known the time the shafting was working. They could tell us if they would,thlt is my minion. Mr. Oulton : lam told the girls would not notice because they have no interest in the particular tables. A young woman named Maggie Whitfield said that no other girls were working at the end of the table 'Where Allen was killed. By the Mayor: Allen was net sent to the table to 'work. She went to assist a man in undoing some wire that was entangled. For the defence the managing director of the firm gave evidence. Be stated that the Filleting had only been coupled up a few days before the accident happened. -Allen had no right to be near it. The shafting was set

in motion without his orders. There was no braiding machinery at that cud of the table. The old shaiting was fenced in according to instructions.

1 Mr. Outten addresied the Bench and said that the Company was in ite infancy, having been in existence only twelve months. It was in the same poaition as an loffender who was a youth, and he submitted that it was entitled to have its age taken into coasideration. It , had had an enormoui amount of success, and orders including Government contracts bad corns pouring in. The business of the company was to make electric cables and vulcanise them. In the hurry all things had not been as they should be. This mac'einery, according to a witness, was not working uetil a day before the acci- dent, and was working more or Irss as an experiment. As soon as it had got going it would have been fence I in. The firm never had notice about the fencing of that particular part of machinery. That was a small point in mitigation of the offence. The shafting was fenced in due course. This was the only table from which shafting projected. It projected a foot and five inches and turned round and round. That psrt of the table was not being used at all and the most likely reason why the girl was there was perhaps, that she was " larking " with one of the men. Major Roe : I think this imputation on the deceased person is quite uncalled for. Mr. Ouiton : She had no right to be there. She must have known this table was out of use and one would naturally think she would keep away from it. The shafting was no doubt dangerous but he submitted these facts for the consideration of the Bench. The managing ' director did not know that the shafting was being worked, As to the question of the girl being employed on Sunday it was nut known to the heads of the firm. One of the subordinate officers invite I the girls to come but it made no difference with their employment. It was not a question of " If you don't come you will get the Back." The reason he (Mr Oelton) was appearing was that the directors of the company did not wish t i acquire a reputation of being careless as regarded their workpeople and did not want it to be thougnt that the cempany disregarded the well being of the employees. Nothing was further from their intentions. The magistrates retired to consider their decision and on their return the Mayor said they were quite prepared to accept the statement of the counsel for the defence that it was not within the knowledge of the directors that the offences had been c-rnmitted and that it was not their intention that anything should be done con- trary to the interests and well-being of the employees. At the same time the offences were so serious and the defence was absolutely nil, that the Bench were bound to come to a decision which, after taking the circum- stances into consideration they thought was reasonable and equitable. In the first case a fine tsf £2O and costs wou'd be inflicted and in each of the other cases a fine of £1 and costs.

div.head: WARRINGTON REVISION COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON REVISION COURT.

Mr. J. T. Foard, barrister-at-law, attendel in the Council Chamber, at the Town Hall, on Monday morn- ing, to revise the lists of voters for the botough. Toe Liberals were representei by Mr. John Clayton, the Con- servatives by Mr. William Holbrook, and the overseers by the assistant overseer (Mr W. H. Woodcock) • The Assistant Town C:erk (Mr. Stanley Wilson) was also present, as well as several of the relieving officers. The total claims, it may be interesting to note, nurisbored 323, and the objeotions 214. The business was of a formal character. Au evening sitting was held at six o'clock.

div.head: MR. PEMBERTON CLAIMS A. VOTE.
div.p: MR. PEMBERTON CLAIMS A. VOTE.
Mr. John Pemberton, of Stockton Heath, claimed a vote in respect of a brickyard and land adjoining at Latchford.

In answer to Mr. Clayton, he stated that he was still a partner in the concern, which had not been formed into a limited company. Toere were two partners—Mr Mainwaring and himself. Mr. Clayton : It is of the right value. The claim was allowed.

div.head: SON AS A LODGER.
div.p: A SON AS A LODGER.

Mr. Harry Mather claimed a vote in respect of rooms occupied by him at 16, Friars'-green. Mr. Clayton : This 13 a case of mother and son. The Barrister: That may be 83. He may be a lodger for all that.

Applicant, in answsr to the barrister, said he occupied two rooms—the front room on the first floor and a bed- room on the second floor. He paid his mother 83 a week. That was for aceomm,Nlation and furnished rooms. He was " in business for himself."

Mr. Clayton : I suppose the rest of the family :have the use of the sitting room? Applicant : No, sir. Mr. Clayton : You have it entirely to yourself ? A.pplicant ; Yes, sir. They come in occasionally.
. , , . . Mr. Clayton : Thn't you get your food with the family. Applicant: No. I have my meals at twelve ; they hive theirs at one o'clock.
Mr. Clayton But you don't have your in?al3 separ- ately on the Sunday? Applicant: Every. day except Sunday. _._ .

Tile Barrister : The claim mot be allowed. It is probable that the rest of the family do come into his room. He could not keep them out very well. •-Mr. Clayton - And the po33iblllt7 is that he would go into the rest of the rooms.
LODOING WITH RH FATHER.

Mr John Atherton applied for a vote on behalf of his brother, Mr William Herbert Atherton, Folly-lane. It was stated that the applicant lived with his father. The rateable value of the hous3 was was £lB 103. Mr Clayton observed that this case V 733 on all fours with the last one. The amount paid by the applicant was 63 a week, It was a Case of father and son.

Applicaot stated that his brother had rooms on the ground floor and one room on another floor. Toe 63 did not include fo)d, it was for the use ot the rooms, His brother was nearly 23 years of age. The Barrister • You Are quite sure that we can rely upon your truthfulness ? You are quite sure be pays your father this rent ? Mr Atherton : Just so, lam not here to say anything that is not correct. My brother went away this after- noon on his holidAys. He received the notico of objec- tion too late. The vote was allowed. The Court was resumed on Taoslay morning. ANOTHER CASE OF "FATHER AND SON."

A son of Mr. William Brooks clairmd a lodger vote. Lie stated that he lived with his father and was a clerk (head of one of tho departments) at Dallam Forge. Be had a bedroom and a sitting-room, and paid his father so much for the use of the rooms.

Queitioned by Mr. Clayton, th 3 applicant said he had not the sole p05i99,173 of the sittinlz-rootn. 113 had three sisters and they also occ igloo:01y made Use OE it. The bedroom, however, was devoted to his exclusive use.: Mr. Clayton submitted that with three sisters in the house the value as required by the Act could not be obtained.
The Barrister said it was running it rather close, but this was evidently a genuine application and he did not like to refuse the vote.
Aoplicant said he bad been on ths rezister before. Mr. Clayton: This is also a CiSe of father an son
The Bairister : That mw b p, but I think the appli. cation is right. I will allow the vote.
" A VERY GOOD LIST."-.--COMPLInENT TO THE ASSISTANT OVERSEER.

Several unimportant implications having been heard, occupying about half an hour. Mr. Holbrook announced that that was all the busi nes% There were no more applications. The Barrister: It is very small work. Mr. Clayton : Yes, we have such an excellent list. The Barrister : It is a very good list. There is no trouble with it. My duties are almost nominal. The Court again resumed its sitting en Wednesday, but the business wasof a purely formal character, known as " starring " the lists.
Burtonwood Parish Council.

A meeting of the Parish Council of Buttonwood, was held on Tuesday evening. The members present were :—Mr. Fairclough (chairman), Mr. Richard Fanshaw (vice-chairman), Messrs Southern, Herbert Gawthorpe, Thomas Mehers, and Fair- dough (clerk) Letters from the Home Secretary were read, suggesting alterations in the prices for grave spaces at the new Cemetery, and after dis- cussion it was decided to fix the charges as suggested by the Home Office. The Clelk was instructed to ask Messrs Gamon and Farmer, the solicitors acting for the Council, to do all in their power to push matters on so that the Cemetery could be declared open at an early date. The Clerk was also instruc- ted to ask Messrs. Gamon and Farmer to arrange for the Bishop of Liverpool to consecrate the Church of England portion at as early a date as possible. The question of bringing water from Collins Green to Burtonwood village was adjourned in order that certain data should be obtained as to cost, &c. It was also decided that those who had applied for the water should be asked to attend the next meeting of the Council, so that the matter could be thoroughly gone into. It is intended to erect an office at the Cemetery to enable persons to make the necessary entries in the Council's books on the occasion of a burial and this question was adjourned in order that price lists could be obtained of an iron struc- ture suitable for this purpose. The question of sub- registrar for Buttonwood was again discussed, the Council expressing indignation at the action of the Warrington Board of Guardians in not assisting them in this matter and it was decided to ask the member for the Newton division to put a question to the Home secretary when Parliament is sitting.

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY, SEPTEMBER 14, 1900.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, SEPTEMBER 14, 1900.

go on in that spirit and continue that good work and make the school more and more a power for good not only to themselves but to others. The more they suc- ceeded and the more earnest and united, they were, the more contagion there was in the school and there would be more attraction for outsiders, and in that way they might draw many who , at present were without any of the happy and helpful associations which they enjoTel in that sch ,01. Re was very glad indeed that Mr. Knowles, one of th 3 veterans of the school had again consented to step into the breach. (Applause). Mr. Knowles was a man whom it

was a privilege to know, and he ha] in many ways of which he perhaps was not aware, helped him (the speaker), both in his preaching and in his work ia the school. There was n 3 man to whom he would more gladly entrust the care of the class and from what Mr. Knowles said he would try to tlk ap the work of teacher until at any rate. Some permaneat arrangement could be made. They were very fortunate in having one of their young men at the helm of the school. Mr Harry Knowles had indeed his career before him, they all liked him, he was the friend of them all, and he was sure that the members of the young men's class meant to support him in every possib:e way. In conclu- sion.he would not say a long G3od-bye because he hoped it would be his privilege to be with them from time to time to look upon their faces and to bear pod things of them. Time and distance could make but little differ- ence when their hearts were bound t3g,ther in deep friendship and in loyalty and good feeling. (Applause.) Mr. Hiu, made a few remarks and hoped they would be able to induce Mr. Drummond to preach the school sermons in April. (Applause). They sometimes forgot the fact that the new building itself was a monument to Mr. Drummond for it was chiefly torough his hard work and his instrumentality that the funds were raised to carry out the building. He wished Mr. and Mrs. Drum- mond every success and happiness in their new sphere of labeur and assured theta that they would always have a resting place in their hearts. (Applause.) Mr. WILLIAM KNOWLES. on behalf of the 1E olian glee party then presented 51r. Drummoad with a photo- graph of the members as a token of their great respect and admiratian for him and deep regret at his depar- ture. As an old chorister he should like to say it would be utterly impossible for a minister to show less obtrusiveness and .t the seine time take a more lively interest in the choir than Mr. Drummond Jid.

The Rev. W. H. DRUMMOND briefly returned thanks. Mr. J. KNOWLES also mad' a short soenh and expressed his pleasure that the first class had unani- mously elected him as their teacher. He wished Mc. and Mrs. Drummond "God speed." The remainder of the ev ming was agreeably spent, a song being rendered by Miss Allen and a part song " Farewell " by the choir.

div.head: THE
div.p: THE
REV. W. H. DRUNEVIOND. Valedictory Sermon on Sunday Evening.
More Presentations.

The Rev. W. Et. Drummond, -vho has been appointed minister of All Soul's, Belfast, preached his, farewell sermon in Cairo-street Chapiii on Sunday evening. There was a large congregation and it being the harvest festi- val, the pulpit and other parts of the sacred edifice had been tastefully decorated with flowers and cereals by the ladies of the congregation. The collection was on behalf of the Warrington and District Nursing Association and a satisfactory amount was realised. The Rw. W. Et. DRUMMOND took fir his text, the words :—" At that time Jesus answered and said, I thank Thee, 0 Father, Lord of Hea7ea and earth, be- cause Thou bast hid these things from the wise and prudent and bast revealed them unto babes." These, he said, were the words of the world's greatest teacher. When they thought of them in that light, they might appear somewhat strange words for a teacher, hut they , contained in then the secret of the influence of Christ. They reminded them how He was always dwelling upon , things which were not reserved for the wise or for the I si:mially gifted, but which were shared by all. Lie did net dwell, as they might have exp cte,l a great te whet* to dwell, upon difficult problems for the intelleo.t.neither did He spend His time in discussing passing controver- sies. It was the common things—the things which all make them feel aud understand—which were the con- stant burd 3ti of His teaching. Cornn in things never were trivial and petty in toe eyes of Christ. It was the

joys and sorrows, the hop's aril duties, of the ordinary man and woman about wtiich He spoke, and as He tculhed them, or.dinary life lost its diiMess, and its sordidness and becamo great, noble and pathetic. It was the same power that wasipossessed by a groat arti-it, as he represented on canvas the common scenes of every- day life—the interior of some cottage li-im , the bedside of a sick child. Whenever He spoke to tinm of common things, He at the very earn moment made them feel His nearness to them,

div.head: Presentations on Monday Evening.
div.p: Presentations on Monday Evening.

There wee an interesting gathering in Cairo-street schools on Monday evening, when toe members of the young men's and young women's classes assembled to make presentations t) the Rev. W. H. and Mrs. Drum- mend, who, during their connection with Cairo-street, have been the teachers of the clasffss. The gifts, which were on view on a table in the centre of the roam, took the form of large photographs of the members of the classes, beautifully framed and reflected credit on Mr. T. Birtles, who hid been entrusted with the work of producing them. The proceedings took the form of a "social " and commenced with the favourite game of " musical chair.' A. glee enti,;43,l " An old rat's tale " was then rendered by the k than quartette and so delighted the assembly that the vocalists were recalled. A dance followed, and afterwards another glee " In a cell or cavern deep " was swig witi great success. Refreshments were then handed round, and these having been heartily partaken of, the presenta- tions took place. _ _ _

Mr. GEortax SHAW said that the next item on the programme was a vary painful one—painful because they were parting with Mr. and Mrs. Drummond—but still there was a touch of pleasure in showing their esteem and love by the pr^sentation of such beautiful portraits as nose on the tab!e. Mr Deurnmonl had been with them for about seven years and had made himself very dear to everyone's fL,art. He (the speaker) was sure that it was with pangs of regret that the mem- bers of both classes parted with him and Mr. Drummond might rest assured that even if he W 3.3 not with them lH body he was with them inspirit ant they should be happy to hear of his success, health and proaperity in his new du ies. (Applause.) He now called upon Mrs. Shaw to present the photo4raph of the young women's , class to Mrs. Drummond.

Mrs SHAW, in doing so, said the phetograph was a token of their love and esteem and to remind .Nlrs Drum- mond of the happy days she had spent in Ceiro-street school. It was their earnest wish that God's blessing would rest upon her in her new sphere. (Applause.) Mrs Dal:mermen, who was received with great enthu- siasm, said she could not tell how much she thanked the members of her class for giving hsr the peotograele. It would be a pleasure to he: to ace thar (ac's every day as rho would whea the photo was hung up in their house at Belfast. It would help her to remember all the Sundays they had sp-nt tog ther. She hoped that in the future the members would c entinue to attend the school, and Miss Houeliton was going to carry on her (Mrs Drummond's) work and she was very glad t think that she would be able to take the clas4. She thanked them very much for their kind thou ;htfulness in giving her the picture. (Applause). Mr. JOHN MONKS, in mitring the presentation to Mr. Drummond on b ,half ot the young men's class, said his: position was full of pain and regret b Tinge, Mr. Drummond Was leaving them, but it v,733 net unmixed with pleasure, because their teacher and minister had been chosen to fill the most irepsrtant position of minister of Alli Soul's, Belfast. (Applause). They were sorry they were losing him because he had not only been their teacher but he had been their sincere friend and they were taking this opportunity of thanking him for all the good he had done for them. The class at present, thanks to Mr. Drummerd'e good leadership, Was in a mast flenrisnlng condition. It was one to be proud of, and he (the speaker) was very proud of teeing a member of the first class, and he was sure Mr. Drum- mond was proud of being the teacher. They had had privileges given to them which had been brought about by his work ; privileges, they hoeld have thought some time ago to be nncor ainablc. Ii t )oo ot the class was better, and Mr. Drummond was not only respected, but loved by every member: in fact they did not realize how much they thought of him until the final parting came. Mr. Drua,mond might tel assured that his efforts had not been in vain. Ils hart new very great pleasure, on behalf of the class, in presenting that most beautiful picture as a small token of tie love, respect and esteem which they had for him, and he hoped that whenever Mr Drummond saw the picture he would think of the happy times he had spent in Cairo-street schools. (Loud applause). The Rev. W. H. DRUMMOND, in returning thanks, said they certainly could not have chosen anything which would have given him more heartfelt pleasure than that most beautiful picture of the class. It was a ales-, won- derful credit te the photographer's art and to their gold friend Mr. Birtles, and he should value it as one of the most beautiful enlarged groups he had ever seen. But that was only a very small part of 'he pleasure real pleasure was in knowing thit the photograph re- presented se much good fellowship and heartfelt affec- tion on the part of the members of the claes. He did not think it would have been possible for any minister to carry away into a new sphere of labour a better gift than that picture. One of his frieede was , saying to him that the picture was as good as a 1 character to him. He (the speaker), thought it was a great deal better, and far more weighty than a great many characters written dowa on paper and in future when the days came, as they did come in every man's _ _ _ _

. „ life, when he felt a little discouraged and thought thiags were not working qeite right and hb wondered whether it was much good working, he should look at that picture and feel rebuked. He had been asking himself many times lately what he had done that he should re- ceive all these presents and that the poopla should he so good t 3 him. He had tried as many others had tried,and as others had succeeded much better than he, to live the life of the scho,l, to throw himself into its life, and to maka its intereite its teach- ing and its sorrows, his own. He felt that he had not altogether failed in identifying himself with thra peholl and whoever might come in his place, ha offend him no higher privilege and no greater gladness in to;s p a !e, than to come into intimate ceetact with the life of the young people in the school It had always been his intention to think only of what was best for thi., school and he had felt that within the last year or two there had been more sense of fellowship, more willingness to serve, mare downrightness and earnestness in the school. He thought that never during the whole course of his ministry there,had he been so happy about the school as he was at the prosent mona-nt. He left it with a regard and affection which he could not express, but he left it also'.with the greatest hopes for its future. They had got magnificent buildines, they had got all the outward advantages for the work which many buildings did not possess. He doubted whether any Sunday School in Warrington or in any of the towns round abeut had got such a beautiful and convenient place. But it was not only the outward advantages that gave him such hopes and confidence in the future of the school, for they had such a splendid band of young people who made it their religious home, the place where they sought their friendships, where they found some of the deepest affectiers of their life, the place where they sought wholesome, happy amusement and serious teaching, and the place where they noerished the delight of doing good to others. div.head: MATRIMONY IN- RURAL LIFE.
div.p: MATRIMONY IN- RURAL LIFE.

Returns show that in the rural districts a heavy pro portion of marriages takes place at a comparatively early age. With little anxiety about employment, and contented with a simple life, We rustic does not hesitate to assume the responsibilities of wedlock. But matri- mony in Arcadia is not without its pains and penalties. A young woman belonging to the village of Sherring- ton, Norfolk, married Frederick Wright, a steady young fellow of Nortleepps, and the happy pair settled down at 105, Mill Hill, Catton, near Norwich. In a short time, however, Mrs. Wright exhibited eerious symptoms of excessive weekeess : she told a Nsrwich reporter who called upon her a very sad story. A short time after the birth of her first child, she was attacked with illness. " It was last September twelve months." she said "that the symptoms began to effect me seriously. I was so depressed that everything became a burden to me, and I had net sufficient energy to on anything. Most of the time I lay in had, and on several occasions I fainted upon getting up. Two months before the birth of my seoond child I was is a very low state from my inability to take food, and the doctor feared it would go hard with me in censoipence• Fortunately I came through my trial safely, bet the old depression returned and con- tinued until the end of last Augur. The President of the Society (Rev J S Hughes) spoke of the work done by the society during the six years it had been in existence, and of the agreeable manner in which the various friends hal %veered toget- her. 4 short programme was gone threugh, during which qoaqi were given by *Rs Mo inftll, Miss Isherwood, and Miss Ada Ground., and recitations by Messrs G Whitfield, and G.
