After tea Mr. Joseph Mounfield said he felt that they, as Free Churches, had been too much separated in the past. They had met that nieht with a twe-fold object, first to eek)sr them- selves in a sociable manner over a pleasant cup of tea, and, secondly, to make a presentation. For some time it had been thought that some acknowledgement ought to be made to their president, the Rev. J S Hughes, for his valuable service., and now an opoortunity had pre• seated itself. Ho hoped Mr. Hughes would appreciate the present they were about to make, not merely for ' Its monetary value, hut as a token of the high esteem in which he was he'd by the members of that committee Mr A J Dunn and the secretary also spike in eulogistic terms of the services rendered be Mr. Hughes to the Band of Hope, and of the groat respect in which he is held in the neighbourhood. The presentation, which consisted of a beautifullyeeoliehed oak stationery eabinet, bore the following inscription. Preeented r 0 the Rev. J. S. Hughes, be the Hill Cliffe and Stockton Heath Unitei Band of Hope, as a token of esteem, on the occasion of his marriage. Sept., 1900." Mr. John Miller, in making the presentation on behalf of the cornmitteeopoke of his personal respect for Mr Hughes, and expressed a hope that he might long remain in the district, to carry on the work he had so touch at heart. Mr Hughes who was taken be surprise) very featly:tele responded, and thanked the friends for the many kind thiees said about him that night, and expeessed his deep gratitude to the committee for the beautiful present, which he assured them would be much appreciated. He had been connected with Band of Hope work from a boy, and his interest in the work had not abated He hoped that he might be able still to work in their midst for many years. He loved the die- trict.and he loved the people.inasmuch as he had chosen a wife from amongst them. The remeinder of the even- ing was given up to game,, &:., into which the younger friends entered heartily, thus bringing to a close a very pleasant gathering.

div.head: RATS AND THE BISHOP.
div.p: THE RATS AND THE BISHOP.

How the rats devoured the Bishop in the round tower on the Rhine—the poets have told the story in verse,and we have all read it in prose. Yes, and both poets and bishops, with crowds of ordinary everyday people like you and me, have felt pains in our stomachs which made us think of the unfor- tunate ecclesiastic of the legend. I mean those " gnaw- ing pains" so often alludea to by dyspeptics who know the whole gamut of that wretched complaint. Mr. Harold Walters says he had these gnawing pains, and tormenting things they are. They come on usually right after eating, and are caused by the contact of food and drink with the highly inflamed coats of the stomach. You see, instead of getting itself properly digested in two or three hcurs, as happens in the case of healthy persons, the food remains much longer in the stomachs of dyspeptics, and starts a chemical action which produces poisons, as in the fermenting process in asks or, bottles or in tne open air. Even if rats were ndeed within us they could hardly do more painful and dangerous mischief. "It was in the spring of 1897," this gentleman tells us," that I began to feel weak and out of sorts. I had no proper relish for my meals, and after eating had gnawing pains in the stomach. After suffering a year in this way, I was completely cured by Mother Seigel's Syrup—taking only two bottles kr all."—Harold Walters, Holt-road, Tranmere, Birkenhead., August 11th, 1898. " I can scarcely ray," writes another man "bow long I suffered from indigestion and weak stomach ; but it was quite long enough. No kind of food agreed with me. After eating had pains in the chest and stomach, end frequently belched up a sour and sickening fluid. I was a good deal swollen round the body, and my breath_ ing was short and difficult. The doctor did what he could, but was unable to help me. " Fortunately Mrs. Craven, an acquaintance, recom- mended Mother Seigel's Syrup, which relieved me so speedily that I was both surprised and delighted. In a short time I could eat freely, and everything agreed with me. lam now in good health, and do not hesitate to admit that I owe it to the use of Mother Seigel's Syrup."—H. Holmes, Sandy Lane Bottom, Allorton, B radford, March 39tt, 1899.

The real rat we destroy by poiso ris, cr catch him trips, as everybody knows. The Euzgested "rats " which gnaw the 3tomach are felt no more after a fewn does of Mother Seiga's disease killing remedy get downi Into the rQeesses where they are ei,ncealed.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. _ Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Chapel.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. _ Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Chapel.
Anniversary Services.

Anniversary services in connection with Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Chapel were held on Sunday and were very successful. The preacher for the occasion was the Rev. Alfred Freeman,formerly of Bewsey-road Wesleyan. Chapel, but now of Harrogate. He preached two ex- cellEnt discourses, that in the evening being based on Lamentatims 3rd chapter, 16,17 and 18 verses. Two anthems were also sung at the evening service entitled : " May God the spring of all my joys,, and "The Title." In the afternoon a cantata entitled "The Ruler's Daughter "was given by the choir under the conductorship of Mr Walter Brough. The connective readings were read by Mr W Bailey. Solos were efficiently sung by Mrs J Tongue, Misses A. Morrell, L Woolley, B Jackson, Mr Parkinson, Mr Dunn, Mr N Cock and Mr Cook jun., Mr T Brough presided at the organ with his accustomed ability. There were large congregations and.the collections were considerably in excess of last year.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

There was an improvement in the attendance at the meeting of this society on Sunday afternoon. Additional members were enrolled, the new members who have joined during the past two weeks exceeding eighty. Mr. Mills presided and in a short address on " Wanted," he showed how at the present moment men and women were wanted to improve the moral and social condition of the people. The P.S.A. movement was one which tended in that direction and he appealed to his hearers to increase its membership and usefulness.—Mr. Treubath, of Liscard, was the spe,ker for the afternoon, and delivered an earnest address on " Work." After referring to the blessedness of work, be pictured an ideal state where there was work for everybody, arid where everybody worked. In order to bring about the ideal state, they must be prepared to pot into practice the teaching of Christ. Referring to some ofithe evils of the prest nt day, he spoke of the drink question and stated that clubs were more per- nicious institutions than public-houses. There were clubs originally intended as eclucatiAnal institutions politically which had degenerated into sly drinking and gambling dens. Clubs needed ending cr mending. Mr. Shaw sang a solo untitled " Come unto Me." The service VMS also taken part in by Mr. George Wallington, Mr. William Beswick and the Rev. John Yong°. It was decided to forward the greetings of the Society to the members of the Liscard P.S.A.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SEPTEMBER 14TH 1900.

IT is pointed out that great War and Social Experiments, wars have constantly led o commercial depression and the postponement of socia experiments. The present war is regarded as likely to do nothing of the kind, because there are large metallic resources in the two Boer States which have been annexed, and a large indemnity may be exacted, sufficient to cover the expenses of the war and to repay the losses to loyal colonists and general property. Butt we cannot be very sanguine as to the repayment o the war expenses. The Boers are not rich men, and they cannot be heavily taxed. The gold mines are not in their hands, and they are owned and worked by miscellaneous capitalists, some British and others foreign. It is not evident that there is any clear idea in this country as to how an indemnity loan is to be raised, and what is the security for its repayment. If the British Government 'should destroy monopolies and re- duce the imposts upon mining enterprise the revenue must fall, and the only hope for the country lies in greatly improved business. The expenses of new administration will have to be met, and with less corruption in official life there will be more officials & pay. The cost of buying up the railways and restoring and extending them, as well as of recouping individuals for their losses, rust create a strained financial situation. It is almost impossible that this country can eseaoe a heavy burden. The troops have to be brought home, there are gratuities to be paid, there will be pensions to bestow, and there are extensive army reforms to to be carried out. We cannot look forward to an easy time in national or Imperial finance. If trade should be depressed under so many bnrdens, with high prices, increasing competition, and flurries abroad similar to that which is now beginning to alarm Germany, the general outlook is not very hopeful. If we escape the pauperism which followed the long Napoleonic struggle, we can haidly escape higher taxation, and this will mean the postponement of useful domestic reforms and many social experiments. What; the working classes of this country have to fear is a period of trade depression, accompanied by high taxation and much sectional distress. There is hope of a boom in South Africa, but it will be chiefly in mining companies and industries. The settlement of South Africa will, in fact, be come less important to many sections of the community than careful finance at home and the continuance of social experiments, the better to . ward off discontent and political turbulence. There is no courage shown in facing this outlook. It is being carefully avoided by the leaders of opinion, and party questions are being preferred to national aspirations. It is an unfortunate pre- dicament, and evil will come out of it if we per- sistently look to the future as if the only impor- tant issue before us is how to deal with two conquered States, whose total annual income would net pay for more than a month's war ex- penses in effecting that conquest. We fear that there is before us a dismal prospect, in which the working classes may have to sutler a good deal, and our finances may get into a hopeless muddle. Political supremacy in Ssuth Africa will hardly have much economic value for years to come, and in the interval we may be doomed to political lassitude at home, and social reforms, without which continued progress is impossible, may be indefinitely delayed. These may seem to be gloomy speculations, :but we shall be glad to haVe something better presented on the other side. At present it is conspicuous by its absence, and we are rushing on with but a poor idea of what is im- mediately before us.

THE London Conference The Press and the of the Institute of Journal- ists will open out some in- teresting discussions on the position of modern newspapers, the ethics of the journalistic profes- sion, and the way in which Fiblic interests are being served under the new order of things. The Institute itself has survived most of the early criticism to which it was exposed, and it has suc- ceeded in developing a mare genial fraternity between pressmen of all nationalities, home and foreign, and a better understanding between pro- prietors and the profession. Accordingly, it must be held to have realised some ot its early aims, and to have knit together all the interests which make journalism what it is—the strongest power in the modern State in proportion to its freedom, purity and ability. In these islands we have no official press, we have no official subsidies, and we have neither a censorship nor an organised Governmental inspiration. Journals depend on their merits for success, and most of them are, in one way or another, the organs of party. There are a few professedly independent journals, and some modern ones profess to have but one leading idea, though in practice they remind us of the old scholastic problem about the number of angels that could stand on the point of a needle. Quite recently there has been a re- vival of the discussion about old and modern journalism, chiefly in regard to sensational tele- grams and the enlarged province given to rumour,

for which the telegraph is inly responsible, though we cannot acquit the public of its anxiety to obtain rumours as well as news. Older journalists can remember the time when foreign news and rumours occupied but a small space, in the journals of the day. The telegraph has changed all that, and not always for the better, because with the increase of foreign gossip the difficulty of detecting the difference between fact and fiction, between conjecture and logical deduction, has been increased. There is hardly time to discrimin- ate in the few brief hours in which a journal must be produced, and hence we have a good , deal printed that can neither be verified nor judged according to the same canons, or with the same ability, applied to domestic news and incidents. But there never was a time when there were more able men in journal- ism, more experts, or a higher standard of thought and action. The British press, political, social, and financial, is unmarked by the corruptions which prevail elsewhere. The political press is free from any suspicion of corrupt influence, and the social journals minister to the craving for per- sonal intelligence without abusing, in a general way, the privacy of the family. If the financial papers, in one or two instances, have not seemed to reach so high a standard the present tendency is decidedly upward. As the world comes nearer together—and that is one of the tendencies of modern civilisation—newspapers become more of a necessity, alike in politics and in business. It may strike some observers as rather odd that the country always accused of insularity should have led the way in this enlightened cosmopolitanism ; but so it is, and the best and truest picture of the world on any one day is still to be found in thet. British Isles. The picture may be wanting in per- fect accuracy, but it is never false and altogether misleading. The newspaper of to-day is, moreover, so enlarging its province that it is elbowing out other literature, and educating the public mind ia a way it never did before. Compare Coleridge's leading articles, as reprinted, with the best articles of any one day in the London and provincial press, and a striking difference will be shewn, all to our credit, and testifying to wider capacity. Defects, of course, exist, and pertness may be taken for VA5'. dom, but, as a whole, the public was never so well served as it is at the present time.

The centrifugal railway which America is about to send over to succeed the stale attractions ot the switchback "appears to be a very formide,ble business indeed. The car, with its load of holiday makers, is pulled by a cable to the top of a very high incline, switched, and sent down a still deeper incline by gravity. A very high rate of speed ig developed, reaching, according to the proud itr ventor, no less than two hundred miles an hour. Then, as if this were not a sufficiently exciting or- perience for ordinary people, the car makes an ur ward leap around a loop, turning a complete somersault—so that for a fraction of a second the people in the car are actually riding head down' wards, with the ground 5O feet below thorn! CO trifugal force, we are told, holds car and people jammed tight to the track above them, and the sensation is over before the young ladies have time to give the shrieks appropriate to such a pus': tion. An American paper styles this" a sort otc 'perhaps' arrangement—perhaps you'4l break , your neck, and perhaps you won't " ; but accordin, to the accounts of the trial trips nothing has be.en hitherto lost except a few back combs from. tne ladies' heads, and nothing broken exCePt a pair o eyeglasses. The writer, with a touch of chara,ct e. istio; humour, tells us there is no intention of .1116, troducing " flip-flau " loops of this kind to varY rf)f monotony ot regular railways. As an adjuoct,ild country fairs we should think the inventioa lOate do quite enough in the way of reduclog - population.

aaid ' Misfortunes never come singly, it is The terrible hurricane in Texas is an instanc! in point. It is one of those great diso,stell which seem to occur in Amorica—the land, °0 "big" things—even more frequently tuad elsewhere. Its victims are not only numbs, by the thousand, but they are not confinen the area devastated by the hurricane. rr-he catastrephe is another blow to La,ncashirso already beginning to suffer from the scare% of cotton. We must deeply sympathise the direct sufferers, the relatives of those Wl' are killed, and the many who have lost their all by the hurricane. But let us not forg'shu Lancashire, on the .industrial classes of whig the virtual destruction of the cotton crop W 1 fall very heavily. Only recently the cottone trade was doing moderately well, ;but 0,5 "statistical scarcity" caused by this Ys3r, poor crop, aggravated by efforts of the sPec,l-5 lators to corner it for higher prices, has 05 already to an extensive closing of mills, the spillne,ra having decided not to buy" spot" cotton " the price came down. Now, however, there is 11 probability of the spinners' action being successt -e, ful, for the hurricane which has passed over tti. cotton belt in the Southern States and nesl ruined the growing crop will create an acts scarcity. The position of cotton previous to t'."o disaster was the worst of any previous year but 0..4 01 during the past quarter of a century, the gent'w average cf the crop on September Ist being 0n../5 68.2-100 representing the average. The Tassr disaster will reduce the new crop to still slentisrld dimensions. The price of raw cotton is alrevjo higher than for many years past; it may rise re- Nmine prices. We fear there are bad times befo,„ Lancashire in the coming winter,and there is liics.vu, to be much distress among its busy hives of ,lbe dustry. For Lancashire has not yet learnt lesson of the great cotton famine of 1861-5 ;
cannot do without American cotton.

Surely the end of the war is at last "in sigite Paul Kruger has left his country and taken refur'd in the Portugese territory; the captain has desetla his ship, and there can be nothing left but for crew to surrender. There is much that is patlife•to in the picture of the greatest man South -§drioi has produced, a fugitive before his enemies. strength of character, and shrewdness of insigin he gradually assumed the leadership of a raceod which such qualities were not uncommon,• s'ffie finally he iwelded that race together until vrt, Transvaal was a country of almost national imehat ance. The State he built up has crumbled; "by only after a marvellous resistance—organissu so the same master mind—to one of the grett.,tl3l6 cr , powers on earth. Paul Kruger is now ad 13'. We are glad of it, and-yet we can pity him ;bp rejoice that international law makes it imPngs;bis for us to interfere with his liberty. A man stamp deserves that the closing days of a career should should end in peace.

- V The Warrington Borough Bench would In ing in the best interests of the town if they fo,ll°;jr,,,f the example of St. Helens maoistratee "e'f.7loi) with applications for music licences in conne°,;ing with public-houses. At the general sessions for St. Helens held last Wee b• the IL' Bench refused to renew all music licences 01,,,D ground that they did not consider it desirable 00 public-houses should be music saloons. The ri'ss
iff

IVen IF4 aood one and a similar decision in War- dugtoi- is sadly needed. At Blackpool, a similar Course has been adopted by the licensing bench Which held that the music licences were respon- sible for a large proportion of the drunkenness. Quite a numberof public-houses in Warrington hold "sing-songs" of a more or less undesirable character and the public-houses thus become a centre of attraction for a purpose which is altogether alien to that for which they are intendod. The granting of a music licence in connection with a public- house cannot be defended on the ground of necessity for the musical tastes of the public are Well catered for by the proper per3ons and through the proper channels. As no valid reason exists for this alliance of beer and music, the refusal of Public-house music licences in Warrington would be welcomed by many and would undoubtedly tend to the raising of the standard of public morality.

div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
A Provincial Letter.

A London correspondent who has the confidence of a large circle of readers as being about the best informed of his class, affects a knowledge of toe "sources of the inspiration " of the "Daily News" about the Dissolution publishel in the early part of the week, and says "they are not first-rate." But the" Daily News" has since found confirmation, it Says, from Liverpool, where the local Conservatives have been warned that the election will be in full awing in the early part of October. It is note- Worthy in this connection that those who do not believe in an immediate Dissolution, are of those Who do no favour it, and had already made pre- dictions of their own to the effect that there would be no General Election this year. Oa the under- standing that where there is much smoke there is fire, both pßrties are sufficiently convinced that, as the Financial Secretary to the War Office puts it, "we are on the eve" ot an election, to continue taking very active preparations in all parts of the provinces.

The Independent Order of Good Templars have this week celebrated their thirty-second National Anniversary at Exeter, with marked success, The Order was " planted "in England, September Bth, 1868, and has now a membership exceeding a hun- dred thousand. Notwithstanding what is being done by this and other Temperance Organisations throughout the country it is known that drunken- ness increases. At the commencement of the century, English people, at home, spent 453 per head on intoxicating drinks. By 1859 it had risen to 003 ; and now the average throughout the country is not less than £2O a year for every family of five, or 803 per head. The national liquor bill last year was double that of forty years ago. Taking into account the increase of popula- tion, it may be replied that this is not convincing. But there are Government returns which are only too convincing, and one does not need to be even a teetotaler :to acknowledge the truths they convey. Germans are popularly supposed to be the greatest beer drinkers; but for every five gallons of beer per head the Germans drink, Englishmen swallow six; and taking all kinds of intoxicating drinks together, the Englishman imbibes twice as much as the American.

The war in South Africa and "trouble "in China 'have intensified the craze for collecting foreign stamps, and it is said that postal officials have not been proof against the temptation to possess them- selves of these mementoes of foreign countries; With the result that a good many recipients of letters from friends in foreign parts have had them delivered minus the stamp. The "provincial ' naturally objects. and the officials should be well aware that, according to law, letters when in the Post Office must not be tampered with. Were these things allowed there is no knowing what mischief Might not accrue, and, for the satisfaction of those Who had begun to lose faith in the authorities it is atated that measFes have been taken to suppress the evil.

It is now many years since Parliament put down night-houses by passing what Mr. John Hollings- head used to describe as the slap-you-and-put-you- to-bed Act. But to a great number of the small shop keepers who eke out a living by selling light refreshments the provisions of the Act remain quite unknown. Indeed, it is questionable whether the !krerage police constable knows what are the lead- ing provisions of the Refreshment Houses Act. Nevertheless, one of the small dealers referred to Was fined the other day at Plymouth for not having taken out a licence. There may not seem to be anything heinous in selling a bottle of lemonade or a pennyworth of fried fish, after ten o'clock at night, but it becomes a crime if the lemonade be drank or the fish eaten on unlicenced premises after the hour mentioned. Many attempts have been made to evade the provisions of the Act by fixing notices up informing customers that they are not to eat or drink their purchases in the shop after ten, and by the owner refusing to supply glasses and plates or anything of the kind. But these devices fre- quently fail, and in parts of the provinces where the Act is carried out with some degree of strict- ness, by the Inland Revenue Officer, there are many prosecutions while in other parts they are scarcely ever heard of. The provi.qon which some smart shopkeepers find most irksome is the one requiring them to close at eleven o'clock and thus lose the late customers.

A good deal has been heard lately, for and against the municipalisation of various kinds of commer- cial undertakings, and possibly much remains yet to he said in regard to some of them, on both sides. But it seems to go without saying that the munici- Dalisation of water and gas, for instance, is one thing, and municipalisation of sport another. Torquay Town Council has done much for the encouragement of:sport. It not only runs tennis, bawling, and croquet greens, some of them at inn- siderable cost, but it makes money grants to support the various clubs associated with the harbour and ganlens. The other day a polo match was to have been played between Exeter Atli Dawlish, and the Council through its nem Committee—these mystifying committees—agreed to provide all the apparatus. and voted 203 towards whatever other expenses there were! Blackpool Town C Ninon has likewise been pushing ahead in the subsidising of sport, the committee which has charge of the amusements haying proposed to thus accommodate one of the local football clubs. But in this case the committee :was not allowed to have its way. Otherwise there 3.8 no knowing, if the example had found imitators in other towns, where the matter might have ended or what consequence might have ensued.

Child labour engaged the attentiou of two widely different bodies, the Trades Union Congress and members of the National Union of Teachers, on Saturday. While both arrived at practically the same conclusion, the Trades Unionists took the larger and more hopeful view of the prospect of further legislative interference on behalf of the Young. All the teachers felt justified in Saying, was that steps ought to be taken to prevent the unnecessary employment of children of school age. An amendment in favour of raising the age of compulsory attendance at school to fourteen years was rejected. But the Trades Congress went the full length of pledging itself to the abolition of child labour under the age of fifteen years. It is surely a sign of the times to find a resolution like this emanating from Oldham; and equally remarkable is it that it was not opposed by delegates representing the cotton industry. A class equally deserving of sympathy is that of the children casually employed out of school hours, referred to at the meeting of teachers fi'.; Plymouth. The lot of some of these children,whose time is divided between Work and school, must bo As hard as that of the juvenile workers in the cotton facteries.

The public have it on the authority of the Rev. W P Sylvester, of Wembley, that nobody ever `! dies," and that the churchyard of Wembley is tree trom the reproach of harbouring the dead. This is how it works, A Mr. Timms wished to erect a tomb- atone to the memory of his father on which to record the fact that his beloved parent" died "on a certain day, and has been told by the Vicar that the obnoxious word could not be allowed to appear. The sorrowing son preferred it to the words" nassed away ;" " entered into his rest,' eszc. But the Bishop of London, on being appealed to. said he could not interfere.

HIGHFIELD TANNERY EMPLOYEES TRIP.

The Highfield Tannery C 3. on Saturday last, gave their employes their annual trip, and tea. About 224 of the men and their wives or sweethearts,left Runcorn by the 8.2 S train for Eby', where an en • joyable day was spent, and returned to Runcorn about 9.30. The trip was also accompanied by Messrs. McKie, J Greenalgh, and Reg; Johnson.

div.head: ACCIDENT AT WIGGS WORK'S, RUNCORN.
div.p: ACCIDENT AT WIGGS WORK'S, RUNCORN.

A boy named Hayes, residing with his parents at Hill Brow, Runcorn, whilst following his em- ploy ment at Wic..tgs Work, fell a considerable dis- tance fro m'one ot the:chambers,and severely injured his forearm, last Monday. Ile was subsequently attended by Dr. McDougall. A WOMAN'S FALL DOWNSTAIRS AT WIDNES.

On Saturday, a woman named Sarah C3ok, aged 50 years, residing at 21, Gossage-street, fell down- stairs and fractured tier left thigh. She was con- veyed to the Accident Hospital, and attended by Dr. Donnelly. MILTON P.S.A., WIDNES. There was a fairly go3d attendance at the usual meeting of this brotherhood on Sunday, when the Pr3sident presided. Mr libwanlock, of Runcorn, swig .` Ora pro noble" and "The Noble Boy of Truth "with good effect. Toe speaker. Mr Starie, gave an excellent address on" The healing of the Demoniac Gaderene," and contrasted man's method of desling with fallen humanity and God's. showed that while man sought to bind and soothe God tried to regenerate and renew the whole. GENEROUS GIFT BY MR. T. S. TIMMIS, J.P. _

Mr. Thomas Sutton J.P., of Cleveley Altenon, ohe of the trustees of St Paul's Church, Widnes, has generously promised £5,003 to tom an endowment fund for tv °nun h, whiei is to be separated frornStAlary's Parish Church. A ziimilar sum will be granted by the Ecclesiatical Commis- sioners,and the Church Council have pleiged them- selves to raise £l,OOO. Mr. Timmis's gift was made through Bishop Chavasse,who has heartily approved of the separation scheme, the present parish of Widnes being one of the latgest in the Liverpool diocese. SAD DEATH OF A WIDNES CHILD —INQUEST ADJOURNED.

Mr. Brighouse, coroner, field an inquest at tin Accident Hospital,on Tuesday afternoon, on the two year old child of John Cardon, 29, Beaumont-street, Widnes, which met its death by falling from a wall lift, high on the Victoria Promenade, on Monday: —Nurse Page said the child was admitted at 4.30 and died at 6.20 from a fracture at the base of the skull. The coroner granted the burial certificate in order that the parents might bury the body, but expressed his intention of adjourning the inquest for a week to enable the Corporation to be repre- sented.

div.head: WATCH STORY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: A WATCH STORY AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Police Court on Walnesday, Mckry Jane Walton, a married woman of New-street, was charged witb having, on the 18th June last, stolen a silver watch and chain, and a silver medal, value 303 from the house of a neighbour named James Molyneux. On the day named Mrs Walton was in Molyneux's house, and the watch, &c.,were missed. Information was given to the police, but although full inquiries were made no trace of the articles were found. The other day Mrs Walton's nephew from Wrexham visited Runcorn and Mrs Molyneux observed thin he sported her husband's medal on his watch-chain. Detective-sergeant Gregory commen- ced inve3tigations which resulted in Mrs Walton confessing she had stolen the articles and had pawned the watch and chain in London-road, Liver- pool.— The prisoner was remanded for the police to make further inquiries.

div.head: CYCLISTS AT CHURCH.
div.p: CYCLISTS AT CHURCH.

On Sunday morning about eleven members of the Widnes Cycle Club attended divine service at St. Paul's Church, Widnes. The cyclists assembled at the Town Hall, and leaving their machines at the rear of the building, proceeded to the church, being accompanied by the Mayor, Councillors Hemingway Laws, and Smith (vice-presidents of the club), and Alderman Sadler. The service was conducted by the vicar (the Rev C E Stocks). The choir gave an admirable rendition of the anthem "He shall feed His flocks," the solo being ably interpreted by Mr W Smith. The Vicar delivered an appropriate sermon. The collections realised ..£2 2s 61, which will be devoted to church expenses. Subsequently the wheelmen were provided with refreshments in the Mayor's parlour, his Worship being duly thanked for his hospitality.

div.p: FRODSHAM.

PAROCHIAL COMBIITTER.—At the monthly meeting of the Parish Wuncil, acting as a Parnchial Committee, held in the Court 11/em, Frodsham, on Friday evening, Mr. C. E. Linaker, in toe chair, it was reported that the Inspector had served a notice to abate the case of overcrowding at Newtown, Frodaham. He had also written to Messrs Kydd and Kythl. Limited,iwith regard to the smoke nuisance at their Frodsham Jam Works. A letter was read from that firm stating that they had adopted means whereby the emission of smoke would be leEmened, the Inspector stating that he had received information from various sources which led him to believe that the nuisance was abated. The Clerk referred to a reso!ution which had been passed by the Joint Water Coinmittee as to the formation of a Fire Brigade, and after disuussion it was agreed to leave che whole arrangement of the details with that com- mittee. The Chairman of the Lighting Committee (Nlr Shore) reported that a tender had been received from the Frodsham Gas Company, ant accepted by the com- mittee for supplying the street lamps with gas duriog the forthcoming season at the rate of 32; per lamp.which report was agreed to. The Water Engineer (Mr Rodgers) reported that he had cleaned out toe reservoir at Over. ton, and the new reservoir erected at Beacon Hill had been filled with water from the mains. div.head: WRETCHED HOME AT GOLBORNE.
div.p: A WRETCHED HOME AT GOLBORNE.
Bad Case at Newton Sessions.

At the Newton P3tt7 Sessions on Thursday before Mr T J Gillespie and other magistrates, Margaret Jones, of Go !borne, was charge] with neglecting her three chil- dren on August 21st and other dates. _

Mr J W Knowles prosecuted on 13,11a,1f of the N.B P.C.C: and stated that on the 21st of August the Inspector Of the Society in con-mu-3y with P.S. Youn.e and P.O. J ,hnson, visited the defendant's house. The Inspecter had received a comoleint fr ma Mr. Paskell,the nuisance inspector for the Golboroe district about the way in which the defendant treated the children. Oa v.siting the house the officers found there was practic- ady no furniture, the beds were rotten, and the place stank to such an extent that Sergeant Young wts sick. There was no excuse for the neglect on the groand of poverty, the de- fendant'3 husletni receiving a wage of 283 out of which he gave his wife 253. 'Tlvr, + wa; ab iy working and he earned 93a wok so that she had Ms to keep the house going with. The rent was 33 31 and she had ample means of keeping the place well furnished and clean. Everything was one mass of filth and dirt. The bed- rooms appeared not to have been cllaned for mohths, the rubbash and dirt being swept underneath the le,ds. The children were well fed but were never clean. The husband woul I have been brought bqore the magis- trates but he had been sent to prison for debt. His in- structions were not to proceed with the charge against the man Toe society felt it was the woman's fault.

Inspector Hackett stated that when he visited the house on the 21st August he found the youngest child naked, awl it was then one o'clock. tier body was copper coloured with dirt, and her head was verminous. Re asked the woman where th 3 clothing was, and she showed him some old dirty rags. The little boy was fairly well nourished hot v try le adiy clotned, and without shoes and stockings. His heel had been cut with some glass and wac vary painful. He was ver- minous and his body was filthy dirty. The elder girl was in a similar condition. In the living room down- stars there were one table, two chairs, and a sofa. The room was very dirty and the on'y fool in the house was a small loaf. Defendant said the children had had their dinner In the back bedroom he &eland a bed on whic4 was a straw mattress with a few old rags and a c:oak for covering. The room was indescribable for filth and smelled abominably. There was no covering I whatevEr on the bed in the front room. On the 6th ins-, he again visited the house but there was no improvement whatever. The bailiff's had been to the house and taken possession of what little furniture they had. The woman was apprehended on Tuesday and the children were taken to the workhouse. On the occasion of his last visit there was a large quantity of goods in the house. William Paskell, nuisance inspector for Golborne, said he had threatened to report the woman many times. He had :eceived cemplaints from the neighbours about the manner in which she treated the children.

PS Young informed the Bench that the defendnnt was a drunken women and was frequently sending for beer. The husband was a hardworking man and bad been gent to prison for debts incurred by his wife. Defendant was committed to gaol for three months with hard labour. PUBLIC 13KNEFIT UNDHR THE CLOCK roaBESF BOOTS in LANCASHIIO.—Advt

RUNCORN NOTES. [By a Correspondent.]

It is not often that I feel disposed to reply to any criticism, unless that criticism is firm and strong and worthy of attention; but for once I wilt depart train the practice of a he-time, so that I may deal with a contemporary's remarks, upon my "lecturing the Urban District Council" on their" cast-iron policy." In my note last week I state facts of which concrete evidence could be produced. In "showing the Urban District Council that their cast-iron policy in the matter of the conduct of the Cemetery and Burial affairs is of ten conducive to the keeping of corpses. above the ground." is the first fact. Fact, number two is that to poor people "a funeral is a decided expense." Fact number three consists of "but too often the .funds for its proper carryinfz out have to be awaited from one or other of tie many burial clubs." Then I say "just because poor people cannot come to the Cemetery Committee office and lay down their fee in hard cash the body has to be lodged for a day and a half longer." Fol- lowing this., the fourth fact, I remarked " Surely there are cases where the Cemetery Committee Officials could relax their cast iron rigidity ?" And, surely, there are ?

How does my critic face these facts? Well in the first instance ha accuses me of "lecturing the Urban District Council on what he (myself) calls cast-iron policy ' ot demanding prepayment of the burial fees." Whereas, wiat I " lecture" the Coancil on, if" lecture " is the word to use, is their "cast-iron policy in the matter of the conduct of the Cemetery and Barials affAirs " which is often conducive tp the keeping ot corpses above ground. The issues are much broader, and my sen- tence implies far more than the narrow- ing down which my critic gives it to " demanding prep lyment of banal fees." Next, my contemporary writer has the audacity to presume what I " :383i1l to think" and argues accordingly. Whereas, I state a positive fact, " that but to often the funds, &c., have to be awaited from one or other of the many burial clubs" Iy critics answers this by saying" burial clubs as a rule pay the demands upon theta very promotly,"-3, palpable admission of my own state- ment of fact. Again, he bogs the ques- tioa ; and asks where the Council should " draw the line."? " They are bound to have a rule of soma sort, and it would hardly be wise to have a debtor and creditor account in matters of this kind" continues my opponent; but he never even suggests wly it would not be wise? It is all abstract and surmise. and the note appar- randy has the ring of an attempt to defend the Cemetery Committee officials from an attack. Well if my coatemporary has a "brief" for the Cemetery Committee it is immaterial to 019. hold one for the public and shall continue to act upon it.

Runcorn ratepayers will find very interesting reading in the report of the Runcorn Board ot Guardians. Amongst other business the Clerk sub- mitted the estimates for the half year, and advised the imposition of a rate of 71- lin the which is an increase of Fl on the previous call. It will be easily seen that the reason for the extra call is a good one,, being for the purpose of maintaining a judicious balance; a course which will tend most materially to keeping the rate at a uniform figure. The call for the Rural District Council is for ,Vid in the be'ng a reduction of 1 in tie .-C on the last half- yeat's call.

Runcorn 11,;herals have further beautified their prerri;:e4 in Regent-street, by baying the interior painted from top t 3 bottom in a very choice manner. This winter should see the clnb•room largely patronised, and the holding of a series of entertainments in the large auditorium downstairs should be ventured upon. A debating Society or Mutual Improvement Society with the object of furthering and fostering Liberal principals would also be useful sad instructive and give many a local aspirant a vent for his abilities. Indeed, unless something of this kind is ventured upon,l am afraid that the usefulness of the club will not increase as it ought to do.

div.head: FASHIONABLE MARRIAGE_ AT
div.p: FASHIONABLE MARRIAGE_ AT
OVERTON.
LINAK SR-TI 1 AIN'S.

It has ever been generally accredited that Overton Church is a beautiful edifice standing in a most beautiful spot, so much so that the visitor is at once struck with the a)sthetic harmony of the surround- ings and pauses instinctively to take in the beauties of nature which form so fitting a setting to the fine. ancient architecture of the church. It is an ideal spot, and nothing unbecoming could be associated with it. •

On Wednesday afternoon, when almost perfect climatic conditions prevailed, the scene in and about this pretty church was one of animation and splen- dour. Almost the whole of the inhabitants of Frodsham, and a good many residents of Runcorn, lielsby and the neighbourhood, flocked there to witness the nuptials of Mr. Charles Ed ward Linaker, junr., (eldest son of Mr. Charles Edward Linaker, F. 5.1., The Rock, Frodsham), and Miss Jenny Blundell Timmins (only daughter of Mr. Thomas Doming and Elizabeth Timmins, 'of Netherton. Frodsham), which were being celebrated, Long before the arrival of the contracting parties, the Church, and its approaches, were occupied by large crowds of well-wishers, testifying to the popu- larity of both the young people's families. Shortly after two o'ctock, the bride, who looked really charming in a dress of ivory Duchesse satin, trimmed with Brussels lace, china, and orange blossoms, and adorned with a tulle veil,entered the church leaning on the arm of her father (who gave her away). She carried a bouquet of lilies, rose, white heather and orange blossoms, the gift, of the bridegroom; and was attended by tour brides- maids ; Miss Jennie Linaker, Miss Alice Linaker, Miss Margaret Fitzbrown, and Miss Lizzie Fitz. brown. The Misses Linaker were dressed in cream embroidered lace over white chiff ma and pale blue silk, and Tuscan hats, trimmed with tulle. They carried bouquets of pink roses,and foliage with simi- lar streamers, and wore turquoi:e and gold brooches the gift of the bridegroom. The Misses Fitzorowe were attired in Lathan embroidered muslin over pale blue silk, with white chiffon hats, and carried baskets of roses. They wore, as ornaments, gold bracelets, the gifts of the bridegroom. The briaes- maids were attended by Mr G Linaker (brother of the bridegroom) as best man; and Mr James Carter as groomsman. The whole party as it ineved up to the chancel, led by the Rev H B Blogg, M.A. (vicar), the Rev R W Ceistoa (curate) and the surpliced choir, to the strains of " The voice that breathed o'er Eden" was most imposing and impressive. Arriving there, the ceremony was solemnly carried out by the ministers named; and at its conclusion, !instead of the usuil homily, the Rev Vicar addressed the young oeuple whom he had just made man and wife,and exhorted them to follow in the steps of their parents, who were both officials of that church, and whom by that marriage had become related. During the ser- vice, which was fully choral, the hymns " Thine for over" (230); "0 perfect love " (578) ; and the " Dens Misereatur " Ps. IxVii., were sung by the assembly. Mr. Hibbort, organist and choirmaster, presided at the organ, and as the happy couple left the Church, after signing the register, the strains of Mendelssehn's "Wedding March," accompanied them. Arriving outside they were literally deluged in a shower of good wishes and confetti. The village generally was en fete, flags and hunt- ing being liberally displayed. Over the entrance to the church was the motto "God bless the happy couple," and another archway en tore'e from " Netherton " to the church wished them "Health and Happiness," and indeed, there was nothing wanting on the part of the inhabitants to assert the genuineness of those wishes. After the ceremony at the Church there was a reception held at Netherton, the following being the guests present :—Afr George F Ashton, Miss Blease, Miss Kitty Blease,:Rev H B Blogg, Dr and Mrs Burton, Mr Boston, Mr:and Mrs Christian, Rev R W Colston,MisslCarter,Mise El and Mrs James Carter Mrs Dewhurst, Mr S:Davies, Rev W Davies, Mr D ouce, Mr E and Miss Evans, Mr and Mrs Fitz- Brown, Miss FAz-Brown, Miss Libby Fif-z-Brown, Miss E Gardner, Mr and Mrs Greg son, Miss Graham, Mr and Mrs T Harris, Miss Heywood, Mr and Miss Huntington, Mr J L and Mrs Tom Jonen, Mr 1.1 N Linaker, Mr Arthur Linaker, air and Mrs If G Linaker, Mr and Mrs C E Linaker, Mrs Linaker, Miss Linaker, Mr Edward Linaker, Mr W G Linaker, Misses Jennie, Alice, and Catherine Linaker, Mr A D Lomas, Mr W B Mills,Mr and Mrs Downes Massie' Mr Alec and Miss Iso Miller, Mr and Mrs Mellor' Miss Parnell, Mr and Mrs W Rhodes, Mr Steward, IMr Jack Smith, Mr Joseph Salkeld, Dr and Miss Selby, Mr and Mrs Snape, Mr Mrs and Ilia Lilian Salkeld, Miss Polly Smith, Mr Mrs and Mr J Stretch, Mr and Mrs W Timmins, Master Leo Timmine, Messrs R.D.. 110., Frank, Arthur and Master Lance Timmins, Mr Mrs and Miss Talbot Mr and Mrs White, Mr and Mrs T Egerton Wilson Misses Ella and Edie Egerton Wilson, Mr and Mrs W H and Mr T and Mr Egerton Wilson, Mr W Worthington, Mr E Wignell, Mr and Yrs J R Jackson. Mr and Mrs T D Timmins.—The catering was by Messrs Bolland, Chester, by whom also the beautiful bride-cake was designed and supplied. Later in the day the newly married couple left for the South of England. and the Isle of Wight, where the honeymoon will be spent. They were accompanied by the hearty good wishes of all their friends. The bride's going away dress was a blue costume, and she selected a pretty Tuscan hat trimmed to match for her head dress.

FOOTBALL.

As expected last week, Runcorn got a severe drubbing from the " Lions," and nearly lost as many points, in the way of goal average, in the one game, as were disc ounted from the whole of last year's total. Whet are the prospects for to- morrow, when they meet the team I fear most? Well, they ore considerably brighter Jimmy Butterworth during the week paid another visit to the Doctors at Liverpool, and has been pronounced ,‘ fit." He will therafore take his place in the usual c3ntre three quarter position. Tloughton and Faulkner to) have recovered sufficiently to don Vie green; and much is hoped for from this quarter of the team. Wilkinson who was injured at Swinton is replaced by D Jones. But perhaps it is the forward rank we should expect most from, on account of the" new blood "included. Last year the home team won the corresponding match by 21 points to nothing ; and, if Broughton reverse this, we shall be disappointed. The full team for Run- corn is as follows :—lbughton, back; C Butter- worth, J Butterworth, Warder, and D lonas, three- quarters: Jolley and Faulkner, halves ; Walker, Reece, Farmer, Gar.er, Lightfoot, Tomlinson, Dixon, and Messenger, forwards.

div.head: RUNCORN WESLEYAN CIRCUIT.
div.p: RUNCORN WESLEYAN CIRCUIT.
Reception of the New Ministers.—A Hearty Welcome.

The Wesleyans of the Runcorn Circuit, on Monday evocinl It, bold a rneetin4 at " Oid Brunswick " for the purpose of cx:endinz to their new ministers, the A. Wells (sdperictendent) and J. B. Foster, a cor- dial welcome. fha proceelings were preceded by a tea, t) which, in addition to the guests of the evening,some tree or four hundred people sat down. After the tables were cleared Mr. A. R. Norman, C.C. (senior circuit steward) took the chair and was supported on the platform by the Rev H Morrison, the Rev A Wells (superintemient),the Rev J B Foster M-ssrs.R H Posnett (junior circuit steward), George Bellamy, J R Frith, J M Frith, S Pope (Haltoc-road), J Looker, S Barrow, C P Bradbury, W Moores (Halton),E Marshall, D Bisbrown,J A Povah, R Mirsh, Mrs Morris, Mr Leach (Weston Pain), Mr thU (Weston), T B xite (society steward St. Paul's), and others: _

After singing of hymn 673 "Come let us j oin our cheerful! Bong; with Angels round the throne," and prayer by toe Rev. H. Morrison The Chairman rematk3d,that all were aware they were met that night for the purpose of according their newly- appointed ministers a hearty welcome. They had been sent to them from the rec mt Conference. That gather- iag he was sure was imbued with a true heartiness of their welcome, and it must naturally cheer the hearts of boll Mr- Wells and Mr. Foster to See so many rally round in that way. He was anxious that they should commence by strikkag the right k3y, and that the right spirit should prevail; and he had been thinking of the punty of the faith that actuated the early Methodists, indeed it was common amongst the early Methodists that they should place implicit confidence and faith in prayer. They used to look upon their ministers as God-sent men, and as having come in answer to their prayers. They would all do what they could to assist their ministers, and if anything was said about them they would not listen to it until it had reaeived full and proper investiga- tion. (Hear, hear.) Finally Mr. Norman wished Mr. Wells and Mr. Foster health and strength in their:three years' ministry,and extended to them in the name of all a very hearty welcome. (Loud applause). Mr. R Posnett said he seconded Mr Norman's words of welcome with a great deal of feeling, because he had seen both sides. (Hear, hear). There was another posi- tihn in the circuit that he filled besides that of junior steward, and it was a polition that he prized more, for in it, it had pleased God to give him the opportunity of preaching the gospel. (Bear. hear.) That was the areatest honour that had ever come to him, and he was sure there could be no higher honour than to be allowed to give one's services to God. (Applause). Oa behalf of the local preachers he also extended a welcome to their ministors, and assured the superintendent that they would take their appointments without any grumbling. (Laue:hter and applause). THE CIRCUIT EXTENSION £2,003, AND MILLION _ GUINEA FUNDS. _

The Chairman said they would now digress from their ordinary prooeedings and give a short account of how the two funds—the Circuit Extension £2,000, and the Million Guinea Funds,—were ptogressing.They had with them Mr J R Frith and Mr J A Povah, the treasurer and secretary respectively of the funds and they would no doubt give them a stat raent of the facts.

Mr. J R Frith observed, in this matter' he did not the Halton-road, bet the whole of e circuit, as treasurer of the Circuit Fuad.So far the money had come in well, but a great deal had been spent.and they were oalv anxious that the other part should come in so that they could go on spending that. (Hear, hear.) Whec the scheme Nam first started they set to work at once, with the result that now the. Weston Paint Schools were almelt completed. Indeed in the course of another three weeks or a month they would be ready for occupa- tion. (Hear, hear.) With regard to Brunswick he believed that had been completed—(no, no)— with re- gard to Halton-road, he was generally asked when they were going to start? He could only reply imperfectly, for they were going to prepare the plans that week and he hoped thee would be able to commence in October. Tue alterations &e., at Preaton Brook had beea specified for and tenders were in so that probably they would be able to start before Christmas. D eating with the fund Mr. Frith said, considerably more thin half the amount originally promised had been paid, and they had a good balance in the bank, though not sufficient to complete the work. Fle could only hope however, that all who had made the promises—and they were all good and true—would pay their treasurer the amounts they bad promised and then they would be able to pay for the work as it proceeded. He was sure when the we-k was completed they would all be pleased. (Applause). He had been told by one gentleman that it would be a pity to spoil the beautiful building in Halton-road. But he felt that a chapel to be beautiful, should be successful ; and what they intended to do for Halton-road would beautify it in that sense. !(Hear, hear). Referring again to] Preston Brook, Mr. Frith added that a site had almost been given them at that place. It was sold to them for only a nominal figure, so in reality was a gift. (Ipplaust). He extended a hearty welcome to their ministers and hoped they would work together in trying to gain success for the church. (applause.) Mr. J• A. Povab, secretary of the 20:h Century Fund, in a humorous address, said his work was far lighter than that of Mr Frith, for he felt on going his rounds for contributions to the 20th Century Fund that he was only calling for his own. (Laughter and appla,use ) ett St. Paul's out of 514 promises there were 315 signatures ; Halton-road out of 263 promises, there were 65 signa- tures. Halton had 221 promises, and 117 .si,guatures ; Csmden 208 promises and 52 signatures ; Weeton, 123 premises.and signatnres:; Weston Point, 41 promisee land 5 signatures.; Preston Brook 11 promises, and 3 signatures. !a several of those places,hewever,he under- stood there were sums of money waiting fer him ; the fecal secretaries had promised to fix a time for him to call for it, but as that date had not been fixed he was still without the money. (Laughter.) The total as remitted to London or in the Bank was £875. or con- siderably over half the promise., thoueh not quite three- quarters. He hoped those people interested %cued take the hint, and if they had money for him let him know and he would make it convenient to call. (loplause ) Mr. Povah also added a word of welcome to the newly appointed ministers.

Mr. R. Marsh (Camden), Mrs Morris (Camden),Messrs Leach (Weston Point), Bell (Weston), T Boo:e (it. Paul's), W Moores (tielton), and T Simister also spoke. The latter eppecially referred to the fact that like Sir William Harcourt, who said he was "an old fashioned Liberal and needed no adjective to qualify!it ;" so he Mr Sinister was" on old fashioned Metholist,"a,nd as stile heartily welcomed their new ministers. The Rev. J. B. Foster said be had INien very much struck with the rem irk regarding Prlvidenle to whice the Chairman had givers utterance. It was not their seeking that he was called to Runcern, and he was sure it was not his own; and he cenld only explain his pres ence as an act of that kind Providence in which he believed. (Applause.) When he was called he made a few inquiries and prayed and addressed his enquiries to the Throne of Grace ; with the result that the conclasion was borne upon him that if he came to Runcorn it would be because the Lord hal sent him. (Hear, hear.) Well, since he had been in Runcorn he had buns looking out far signs of encouragement—(hear, hear)—and was pleased to say he had found them. (Applause) The first thing that encouraged him was the knowledge that he was following a man who had been loved very much, and he was thankful to stand in the place of a man who stone] high in their affections and esteem. (Applause.) Another sign of encouragement he noticed was the deep spirituality of the circuit stewards. He thought it was always a good thing when circuit stewards were good business-men with a keen sharp eye for pound-. shillings and peece ; but it was far more encouraging when they found that the c'rcuit stewards had a keenness also tor the spiritual things. (Applause.) Ile was perfectly satisfied that in the present circuit stewards they had men who deeply appreciated spiritual work ; and he felt thankful for what Mr. Posnett said because it would lead to suc- cessful work in the circuit. (Applause.) He had also noticed how very hearty and industrious their people were. It was evident it Was not going to be a" one man show" in that circuit—(applause)—and he did not think either in Camden, Weston, or Weston Point they would expect him to do all the hard work. (Hear, hear.) Rather he thought they would all willingly put their shoulders to the wheel. (Applause). He would now ask their forbearance for a moment. He had during the past week been exercising himself in what he described as the Parliamentary exercise of " catching the speaker's eye," that was, as he walked up and down street he had been endeavouring to catch the eye of every Methodist. (Leughtcr). 0! course he could not know them all, but he took it they all knew him, and he was on the lookout for the bright smile of recognition which would lead to the exchange of " Good morning ! " (continued laughter). Whilst in Runcorn he wanted to be on good terms with the young people, and althoueh Mrs Morris had said all the mothers of Camilen were in love with him," he was not going to give 4.11 his love to them (Laughter). But he would say this, that if ever he expected to have a good time it was at the mothers meeting at Camden, (Continued laughter). Still he wanted to have a geed time with the young ones elsewhere. (Hear, hear.) He did hope the young people would give him their confidence, as there was nothing he loved better than to helps young man or woman to take a firmer step for Christ. (Armlatiee). Continuing, Mr. Foster spoke of the joy of a Christian's life, and urged all to do their best for the schools and the church. With regard to visiting he would visit the " well "as often as he could ; but thesick would have his especial charge, and he would take it as a kindness to be called to see them no matter what the hour of the day or night. (Loud applawr). Grumblers he never took any heed of, hut would always be willing to listen attentively to all that any member had to say, even if the ideas expressed could not be adopted by him. In conclusion let their motto be "all for the Church and none for himself "and he felt ante the hlesring of God would rest upon their work. He thanked all for the hearty welcome. (Loud applause).

The Rev A WEees (superintendent), who was most cordially received explained as his reason for requesting the Rev J B Foster to address them first, that he felt there were some things which ought to be mentioned. If he had spoken first and left it to his colleague to take them up they might have been overlooked, new he was in the position to endorse all that his colleague had said and:proceed on other lines. (Hear, hear.) He did not sup- pose that Runcora had the slightest interest in himself or he ha the town until he had received their letter of invitation. It was a marvellous letter and concluded in terms beautiful and simple. It was not one of those letters in which everything was represented in the most rosy colours that he received from Runcorn, and though he had received other.] offering considerations which Runcorn did not—considerations by no means to be despised—still he felt that somehow he " cottoned" to Runcorn, if they would allow him to use that most expressive term. (Applause.) And since he had posted his letter of acceptance he had never had the slightest wavering, but rather felt like one who had done the right thiag,and came with a deep and thorough conviction that his sojourn in Runcorn was going to be a happy period of labour. (Applause.) Having ex- pressed his obligations to the stewards and stewardessis for their many kindnesses to him and his family upon his arrival, Mr. Wells paid a high tribute to the cleanli- ness and regularity he found his house in, and also to the order in which the Rev. C W L Christien had left all that was handed over to him as Superintendent. I Indeed he did not think there was one thing that gave him the slightest tinge of regret. (Applause.) He desired first to thank them for the very hearty welcome they had extended to himself and his colleague. (Ap- plause.) The Conference had placed toe res- ponsibilites of superintendency upon his shou'ders, and at the outset he wished it to be under- stood that he was going to be the superintendent. (Hear, hear.) He would have to be consulted first in all things, and the arrangements made afterwards ; not the 1 arrangements first and the consultation afterwards. (Laughter.) He urged all to be united and work for the 'same end " the upholding of the aCtoure.h of Christ." I He too, was an " old fashioned Methodist," but he be- lieved in the principle of supporting a cycle club, a tennis club, a fuotball club or any association that had for its aim the furthering of the churn, Young people would congregate together and he felt it was good for them to congregate,and be bound together in an associa- tion of that kind. The object of all was to build up a living church, and football, cricket, or whatever it I was would have his support ii it tended towards the building up of such a church. (Hoar, hear.) But if they did not tend to that they would get no sympathy or support from him. (Applause.) He urged all to give more attention to the celebration of the Sacra- ment. The attendance at Sacrament was not what it might be, and it had pained him to find that out of a membership of 198 not 25 per cent. had stayed to the Sacrament upon the last Sunday. He would remind all that the Sacrament:was instituted by the Lord Jesus Christ himself, and all who neglected it were cutting themselves off from a most comforting means of grace. (Amen ) If every family only sent one representative a month,he was sure they would have a far larger attend- ance than they bad at present, and surely that was not asking too much. (Hear, hear.) He reminded them of the Prayer Class and other meetings, and though their meetings were so many that they could not all he attended it was well worth'an effort for those who could make use of their opportunities and go as often as possible. (Applause.) They would of course have to beg occasionally for money and for workers, and whilst referring to that he was reminded of what one of his friends had written to him, in anewer to his query as to how he had got on at his mission. His friend wrote "I get Into their hearts, and then I got into their cash." (Laughter.) Well, he wanted te get into the hearts of all Runcorn people, but it must be they who should open theirs to him, and if the 7 loved him, and he loved them, and they both loved the Lord Jesus Christ, be felt sure his ministry amongst them would be very happy and prosperous. (Loud applause.) The meeting then closed and the Benediction was pronounced by the Seperintendent.

div.head: AGAINST VACCINATION.
div.p: AGAINST VACCINATION.

The D Irby Union requested the Runeorn Board to adopt and forward to the proper quarters a series of resolutions they had passed with regard to the'Vaccina- tion Acts. The resolutions affirmed the belief that the time has come when it is no longer necessary to retain upon the statute book a law making the vaccination of infants compulsory. that the medical faculty are not agreed upon the effect of vaccina.tion in preventing smallpox, that isolation hospitals and improved sanita- tion are the main factors in preventing the occurrence of smallpox, and if former conditions were allowed to obtain no amount of vaccination would be effective in preventing the disease or stopping its spread ; that: Com pulsory vaccination is no-English, and it Guiorcement, by state appointed officers, tvr..7.hical and repellante that it is unnecessary ie ricoved by the absense of diseasd even in the letst vaccinated districts where isolation ant sanita:ion is enforced, that it is costly and unjust that is is inoperative seeing that seven-eighths of the births available for vaccination during the past six months are still free from the operation of the lancet and lymph of the public vaccinator,and finally the hope was expremed that the injustice and anomoly of the Acts might be modified if not accept away. Mr Linaker proposed and Mr Mzlntyre seconded that the communication be laid on the table.

div.head: THELWALL NUISANCE.
div.p: THE THELWALL NUISANCE.

Mr R A Naylor Cuerden Hall, Thelwall, wrote under date September :—"Dear Sir' I am much obliged for your letter promising that your Council will keep the tannery nuisance under observation. Your medi- cal officer has called upon me and stated what yo a were going to have done :—(l),' the tannery effluent thoroughly purified ; (2), the brook covered over; (3), ventilating shafts at both ends of the culvert passing under the canal ; (4) the pipes along the boundary extended beyond our gardener's house. I should be glad to have these matters promptly attendel t ) as the smell has been most offensive during no present week; in fact an expert we had over on Tuesday last in his report dechres we are in continual danger of fever and diphtheria.l have kept your medical officer fully informed this week, and he is quite at linertv to read my letters as they nrobab:y will bo made public Liter on: To G F Ashton Esq , Runcorn."

The Clerk said the Council had n;Ver determined to do the work mentioned by Mr. Naylor. Dr. Adams said Mr. Naylor bad quite got a wroirg impression. What he (the doctor) told Mr. Navies waS that be had presented a report, iu which he bad sugges- ted what should be done. He never said the Council bad decided to carry out the sinrgestions. Inspector Farrington vett Mr Naylor was asked if these things were done would he be satisfied. The Clerl said Mr Naylor appeared to have misunder- stoi the Medical Officer, and he had been informed that he was tn;st.ken in supposing that the Council had resolved to do the work be mentioned.

Inspector Farrington said with respect to the extension of the pipes to the gardener's house, MC Naylor put its those pipes, and if be wanted them lengthened he must do it. The Council had nothing to do with ir; at all. The Clerk was instructed to reply to Mr. Naylor in the way he suggested.

COWSHEDS AND DM ET REGULATIONS.

The Inspector reportei upin expired notices served upon farmers under the Dairy and Cowsheds Regula— tions. The cases he mentioned were in the township of Alvanley, and he applied for an extension of time in order that the persons concerned might comply with the suggestions made. Ho prvosei to report upon other townships at successive meetings of the Council. There was an idea abroad that these regulations could not be insisted upon, and he suggested that the Council should support his action. The Chairman asked if they could compel the tenants to do the alterations to cowsheds, So. The Inspector said they would have to summon the defaulters before the magistratas. He (the inspector), considered it was a hardship for the tenant to hive to make the alterations.
The Chairman: lam afraid you will have to take a good ma I.y tenant farmers before the magistrates. This was all the business.
