The annual report states that the profits for the year ending June 30,1900, amount to £123, 644,and the balance brought forward from last year is. £7,626, together £131,270. An interim dividend at the rate of six per cent, per annum was paid on both preference and ordinary shares in narch last for the half year ending December 31, 1899,amount- ing to £24,920, and the directors now recommend that for the past half year a dividenu be paid at the rate of six per cent. per annum on the preference shares and a dividend at the rate of 14 per cent per annum, making, with the interim dividend, 10 per cent fcr the year, free of income tax, on the orain- ary shares ; this will absorb £49,595 The directors further recommend that £28,609 be written of the coliiery leases and goodwill account, and £20,000 added to the reserve fund, and that the balance, £8,146 be carried forward. The directors have given notice to pay off the £3,000 mortgage on the new workmen's cottage at Coppull. The full amount of £3 per share has been called up on the 6,60 pre- ference shares issued last year. The binkings at the new Coppull collieries were completed in April last and a large output of coal from all the workable seams is now being produced. The course of trade during the year was marked by an unusual degree of activity, and in all departments of the Com- pany's business the results are satisfactory. Of late, however, some reaction has overtaken the iron and steel trades,the ultimate outcome of which it is at present difficult to foresee.

div.head: EXAMINER, PRIDA/ SEPTEMBER 14,1900.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, PRIDA/ SEPTEMBER 14,1900.
RUGBY FOOTBALL.
St. Helens v. Rochdale Hornets.

Before 4,000 spectators at St. Helens. Rochdale kicked off, but no return was made. Passing between Boyle, Barnes, Traynor, and Liversage gave St. Helens a footing in the visitors' quarters, when Traynor later dropped a goal for St. Helens. Crossing over Trayncr started for St. Helens, Hodgkinson returning, Doherty later kicking out of play. Rochdale were then con- spicuous with some good back play, the venue later being in the home 25. Play eventually settled down at centre, and was evenly contested. Near the clo.e of the game Blincow scored an unconverted try for Rochdale, tut nothing accrued. Final .—St Helens, ten points ; Rochdale Hornets, three.

and led by Bartley and Morgan t'aey bombarded the visitors' goal. Bartley got in a splendid sholfrom long range whic trlvor savcd at the expense ef a co':aer. This was accurately placed by Morgan and after an excitiog scrimmage in the goal-mouth Settle wlfzzed the ball through a sea of legs past M'lvor, thus making the scores level half-an-hour from the start. Both ;lidos now fought stronously to give the lead and the de':( aces on either side were severely tested. II )wever the in terval came with the score one each. _

On resuming with the sun at their backs and the hill in their favour the homesters soon began to make things hum. Splendid work by Bartley and Morgan resulted in the latter forcing an abortive corner. The ball was seen again bobbing about M'lvor and the Darwen goal bad some marvellous escapes. Bartley brought M'lvor to his knees with a beautiful grounder and before he could clear Morgan was upon him. The custodian, however, managed to scoop the leather round the past and into touch. Following this Bartley and Morgan Instituted a nice passing movement down the wing,the latter finishing up with a nice centre which, however, Linton and Leach just failed to reach. A breakaway by the visitors was not of long duration and a brilliant run along the line by Settle which !oak ,d promising was spoiled by that player being badly fou;ed within the twelve yards line. After deliberating for a short time the referee awarded a penalty and this was safely placed into the net by Settle. There was no holding the ' homesters in after this and Darwen rarely crossed the half-way line. When they did ,they were easily repelled, the efforts of their forwards lacking method and although the Earlestown backs core far ' from clever they had no difficulty in dealing with these spasmodic bursts. Before the close Linton added a third goal after the scrimmage under the bar. The form , shown by the Earlestown team was a vast improvement (on the previous week's dispiay and if they maiatain it they will win more matches than they will lose. The inclusion of Bartley in the forward line made a tremend- ous difference and when this player gets in proper work- in order he will be one of the best forwards in the Lanca- shire League. His individual play on Saturday was splendid and he fed Morgan unselfishly. He is exceed- ingly quick on the ball and is tricky enough for any company whilst he rarely ehot wide of the mark. Chew was the shining light in the home defence. He kept goal with remarkable ability although he had little or nothing to do in the second half. The backs were fair but if they wonld get the ball away and not try so much fancy work they would come off a great deal Letter than they do. The half backs as usual were in fine trim Whitehouse being about the pick. He worked like a horse and was here there and everywhere. The forwards were in great form an although Leaton is practically no use in the centre, they were far and away a better lot than the opposing quart- ette. If Linton had utilized all the chances that came his way, Earlestown would have won by a larger margin than they did. When be gets a pass, he kicks the ball straight in front of him instead oi banging It out to his wings. The visitors were outplayed at every point of the game. Tee best man on their side was the goa'-keeper, Mivor who played a sterling ganae between the sr,iake. ro-morrow Earlestown visit Chorley, and they will do well if they manage to make la draw of i.

div.head: Wigan V. Widnes.
div.p: Wigan V. Widnes.

At Wigan before 3,000 spectators. Wigan defended well against the wind and sun, and then Anderton placed a penalty goal for the home sidc• Half-time score :—Wigan, one goal, (two points); I,Vidues nothing. Od resuming Widn:s attacked strongly, bet were re- pulsed, and Ball ran ovr with a fine try for Wigan. Batey kicked judiciously for Widnes, but Nicholson ran in another try for the home club. Final score :—Wigan one goal and two trics ; Widnes, nil,

div.head: Barrow v. Oldham.
div.p: Barrow v. Oldham.

The former's ground at Oldham was the Fcene of a close and exciting contest between these fifteens. 'the visitors, however, proved the stronger—victory resting with them by two tries to one try. Stockport v. Millom.
A win for the home side by two goals and two tries to nil was the result of this contest at St, ckport. B !van kicked the go,tls. and Silvester and. Robinson ran in the tries after some smart play.

div.head: Leigh v. Broughton Rangers.
div.p: Leigh v. Broughton Rangers.
Leigh, playing upon their own ground, beat their opp,nents in the first stage of the struggle, and led at the interval by a goal and throe tries t 3 nil. Finally they won by eleven points to two.

div.head: YORKSHIRE SENIOR COMPETITION.
div.p: YORKSHIRE SENIOR COMPETITION.
Leeds v. Batley.

In the presence of about 7,000 people a keen struggle took place between these clubs at Headingley, Leeds. At the usual interval the;score was one goal and one try ail, but in the end B itley won by two goals and three trie3 to two goals and two ttis. Davies, Sowden, Fozzard, Jagger, Law. and Daley played conspicuously for their respective sides. Bradford v. Huddersfield.

Playing upon their own ground, before a large assem- blage, the Bradford fiftfen woo this game, after PI g()0(1 struggle, by three goals and three tries to a try. EAgers Frank Murgatroyd, COmpton, Mared,2n, Pollard, and Wood were prominent throughout. Hunslet v. Liversedge.
In the opening portion of this game at Hamlet, A. Goldthorpe scored a goal and Hannah a try for the home selection. Daring the course of the second moiety th: _ _
brothers Goldthorpe each land2cl a goal for HunsleE,who won by nine points to nil.
Bramlev V. Brighouse Rangers.

It was not until the secoad half of this game, at Bramley, was well advancei that anything tangible was accomplished, and then the Rangers secured a try, which was improved upon. This eventually gave them the:victory by five pints to nil.;

div.head: Wakefield Trinity v. Leeds Parish Church.
div.p: Wakefield Trinity v. Leeds Parish Church.

At Wakefield, play was interesting prior to half-time, and during this period Davison scored a try for the visitors. Afterwards the game became very monoton- ous until "no side" left victory with Leeds Parish Church by,three points to nil. Holbeck v. Halifax.
These fifteens were associated in a very evenly con- tested game at Holbeck. EAch side scored two goals and a try, and a draw of seven points was the result. Castleford v. Hull Kingston Rovers.

The play went greatly in favour of the Rovers, at Castleford, awl a victory awaited them by three goals And a try to ni!, a result chiefly due to the good play of Stalks, Ward, and Tullock. Hull v. Manningham.

At Hull the home side had the better of the openim-,• half, and led by a goal and two tries at the change of ends- Subtequently the visitors scored a goal and a try to their rivals two. Hull thus won by eleven points to five. -

div.head: " A".ITEANIS COMPEI ITION. RUNCORN "A 'v. SwiNTom "A."
div.p: " A".ITEANIS COMPEI ITION. RUNCORN "A 'v. SwiNTom "A."

Swinton"l-A—;;--ls-iroug—ht a-titrong combination to Run- corn last Saturda.y,in the hope of gaining" two points" in the" A" Divi,ion ad the Lancashire League. Con- sidering that the home team had been drawn upon very largely to fill vacancies againnt Swinton at Swinton,little hope ,of winning filled the breasts of the small home crowd that turned out to witness the game. In the first half Shepley scored a try fir the visitors, and two others were run in, but disallowed ; Sufficient proof that Swin- ton did most if not all the pressing. Just before the interval, however, Richardson the home back, dropped a fine goal. Re-c-marnencing with a point behind, Runcorn played a far superior game to what they had hitherto shown, and at times Swinton were hardly pressed. Each team, howevor,held their own until time wt.: approaching. Possibly, under the impression that their int; Tam sufficient Swinton then played an easy going defensive g.:.lPP,anl took their time about dropping out, Just before the enu, however, Runcorn tucked up and Weston getting possession 13,3,-,rd a brilliant try. The kick at goal failed. It was too late n 0.7 for Swinton to wia and the game ended : Runcorn, 1 goal, 1.Z.7,7! 5 points ; to Swinton, 1 try, 3 points.

div.head: FLETCIIER Ruz;sELL's V. STOC.HPORT "A."
div.p: FLETCIIER Ruz;sELL's V. STOC.HPORT "A."

The Cheshire men opened the new ground of the former on Saturday last. The home team kicked off against a fierce sun and moderate wind but not with- standing good play on the part of Clare, Foster and Paden could not break through the defence of the vi,iters which was 'very good. Galt-time arrived with no score. Upon change of enia the hJmesters quickly got to work arid C)rless scored an unimprov, d try after pretty passing by Foden and Clare. It was fitting that an old St. Mary's Club player should thus score the first try on the new ground of the Gas Engineers. Not to be denied Foster, with a strong run got over but no goal resulted. The game ended in favour of the home side by 6 points to nil who thus maintained their capital form against Tyldesley the previous Saturday.

LATCHFORD BANGERS V. BIRKENHEAD WANDERERS "A."—This match was played at Latchford on Saturday afternoon, in fine weather. Latchford kicked off, and play was for some time in favour of the homesters. A fine dribb:e by Birkenhead forwards took the play to the centre, where a series of scrimmages took place. A free kick for Birk-nhead was given in the Latchford quar- ters, Snertatt relieving with a fit.e run. Birkenhead were not to be done, for they went down again, J Davies rushing over. The kick at goal failed- After this reverse Latchford got down in the visitors' half, Sherratt missing a certain try. Birkenhead then pressed, Knight scoring, but n oal resulting. Half-time t—Birkenhead Wanderers " A," six points ; Latchford Rangers. nil. During the sEcond half the home side scored a try which was not improved upon,and the Wanderers thus won by six points t.) three.

div.head: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL. LANCASHIRE LEAGUE. Earlestown v. Darwen. Earlestown Win Splendidly.
div.p: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL. LANCASHIRE LEAGUE. Earlestown v. Darwen. Earlestown Win Splendidly.

For their second match of the season Earlestown made several departures from the team, which was 93 easily overcome by Staly bridge Rovers in the opening match. Clibborn was unable to play, and this let in Whitehouse at left half, and ne Barney's transfer bad been obtained he played right inside vice C Linton. Owing to the counter attraction of the Lifeboat Demonstration, it was anticipated that tha attendance would be meagre, and this proved to be the case ; only about 300 spectators lining the enclosure. The weather was beautifully fine from the spectator's standpoint, if a trifle too warm for that of the players. Losing the tdss, Earlestown started against the hill and facing a brilliant sun. The pace at the opening was far too fast to last long, and it soon began to tell on the players. The home front line at once got up but Leach ran the ball over the line, and from the ensuing goal tick the visitors paid a brief visit to the borne goal. They were however pulled up before they became really dangerous. and a magnificent piece of work by Bartley enabled that player to get in a perfect centre which dropped clean at the feet of Settle. This player had the goal at his mercy, but be dallied too long and his shot was charged down. The visitors were soon again troubling the home defenders and it was, more by good luck than good judgment that they were prevented from scoring. The forwards were allowed far too much scope by the home barks and Chew had as a consequence to be con- stantly on the alert. On one occasion he had to deal with a hot 'an from the right 'Ring and his clearance was met and banged back again, the custodian just getting his fingers to the leather and tipping it over the bar. The ensuing corner led to another fierce onslaught on the Earlestown goals in welch Chew figured promi- nently, clearing shot after shot in masterly style. At length the pursistence of the Da,rwen forwards was re- warded, Cooper banging the ball into the net4rom a corner. This success, whica came after the game had been in progress twenty minutes roused the bomesters

div.head: NORTHERN UNION. LANCASHIRE- SENIOR COMPETITION.
div.p: NORTHERN UNION. LANCASHIRE- SENIOR COMPETITION.
Warrington v. Salford. Brilliant Game at Wilderspool.

The football season at Warrington really commenced on Saturday when Salford were the first senior corn- petition visitors to Warrington. They, like Warrington had won the opening match of the season the previous week and no doubt expected to win again. In this they were disappointed, however. The day was a splendid one for the game,albeit a trifle warm,and the spectators rolled up in large numbers till there must have been quite 5,000 round the enclosure. Both teams turned out as selected and blth may be said to have teen strongly represented. Mr. B. Ashton (Werneth) was referee,and the tegms lined up in the following order. Warrington : 11.11 am, full back ; Fish, Isherwood, Lawless and Hoclonhall, three-quarters ; Burgess and Duckworth, half backs ; Taylor,Morrison, Eden,Scholtz Boardman, Swift, Moreweather, and Andrews, for- wards.

Salford : D Smith, back ; J Aldred, T Williams, WI Crscker, and A Pearson, threequarters ; I Grey and B Griffiths, hall-backs; J Rhapps, J Williams, P Tunney, R Shlw, NI Gledhill, EI Buckler, J Worthington, and G F shsr, forwards. Warrington were fortunate in the spin of the coin, and took the advantage offered by wind and sun in the first hill. Griffiths set the ball in motion for the visitors, Meraweather failing to respond. Salford thus got a -tin(' in the home half, from whence they took a lot of removin;. Holding a big advantage in weight forward they carried scrimmage after scrimmage, but the keen tackling of the ia;:ttne backs prevented them making much headway. The.; rushed the ball to the line how- ever, and Warrington owe:I everything to a brilliant el arance by Hallam. Then the ;.;:.,me forwards broke loose and tested Smith, the visiting back being grassed by Fish. Salford again got possesFien, awl a bout of pass eg was well followed up by Warriegtou, Law- less knocking Pearson in touch. Another effort failed through Williams bungling Griffiths' pass. The first quarter passed without event, but with the Beds still pressfrig hotly. The fast pacs was beginning to tell, and Warrington showed up better, the forwards invading the Salford half with grand rushes. The 111 l gave way before the onslaught, Taylor and Andrews making a determined effort to get through. A penalty kick did not improve the position of the visitors, and they had an anxious time. Fish raced up after a cross-kick, and failed by inches Cray to drop on the ball. Pearson attempted to punt clear but gave Flockenhall a mark near the line, Fish landing a lovely ,goal from the place. Warrington's vigorous attack was thus early rewarded. The reverse vus'd the ire of the Reds and they quickly rushed to trio other end. Smart passing by Griffiths, Williams, and Alired resulted in the last-named crossing at the corner after being in touch. The try was allowed hewever, a, d Shaw kicked a fine goal from a difficult angle. Warrington were now three points be- hind and immediately went off with a great rush. Hal- lam replied to Griffiths and the latter mulling Mere. weather romped over beneath the cross-bar, Fish giving the homesters the lead by a goal amid great cheering. Warrington were now going very strongly and gave the heavy Salfordians no rest at all. The visitors' line was sehjected to a hot attack. Hoekenhall putting in some effective work on the right. Fish was also cheered for a brilliant run over half the field, his progress not being stopped until he had dodged fouernen in succession. Half timelirrived withr he score reading,Warrington 7 points, Salford 5 points. Taylor re-commenced, and the Warrington forwards soon had possession, Boardman making a dashing run into the Salford half. The Reds played with desperate determination, but they had more than met their match. Fish stopped Aldred easily when the wing man got going once more. Warrington kept the upper hand, and Hoekenhall scored a pretty try at the corner as the result of fine eombination between Law- less, Burgess and himself. Fsh failed at goal, but as Warreag,ton were a clear 5 points ahead this did not matter much. Warrington were several times forced to defend, and on one ow scion Fish aroused the utmost enthu-iasm by snatching the ball and running three- quarters the length of the field, only failing to score through stumbling when dodging Smith, and thus losing speed. It was a fine effort all the same. Both sides were straining every nerve, and Board- man saved well on the line for the homesters. From a scrimmage near the pests the Salford hacks cot possession and the bell travelled rapidly to Pearson who was only grassed at the earner flag. Then Williams made a dashing run and was stopped in the nick of time by Hallam. The Reds did not go alto- gether unrewarded for the attack as Burgess kicked straight to Smith, and the latter dropped a goal. War- rington rallied again and Salford were driven back to thelline, Fish making fine progress on the wing, only to be hurt in the process. The Salford forwards showsd signs of distress while their opponents were remarkably fresh and energetic. Boardman almost led to a score by charging the ball down. Salford defendrd well but their efforts in the other direction were promptly checked by Isherwood and Hallam, who mark ,d very judiciously. Time arrived with Warrington the winners ef a grand game by 2 goals 2 tries (10 point 3) to Salford 2 goals 1 try (7 points). Swinton v. Runcorn.

At Swinton. There were fully 8,000 spectators present to witness the meeting between last year's League cham- pions and the Challenge Cup champions, and a good game was anticipated, but, unfortunately for Runcorn, three of their belt players—Houghton, Faulkner. and G Butterworth—were unanle to play, through injuries. The absence of such sterling players riot only robbed the game of much interest but materially weakened their side. The result of the play was a decisive victory for Swinton by 17 points to nothing. Jolley who acted as full back for Runcorn, played a grand game, and but for his strong defence the score muse have been much larger. In the first half of the game Hampson gained a try early on, then Davies scored from a strong run, and just before the interval R Valentine added the third try, none of which were improved upon. In the second portion of the game the visitors played up strongly, but the Swintoniars gradually wore them down, and in quick succession Messer and James Valentine scored trios for Swinton. One try only was improved upon by ; Valentine. Final score :—Swintkm, one goal and five tries (17 points) ; Runcorn, nothing.

div.head: CORPORATION EMPLOYEES BLAMED.
div.p: CORPORATION EMPLOYEES BLAMED.
The Shocking Accident to a Child.
Inquest and Verdict.

Mr. Bris,-housd conducted the adjourned inquiry in the Parade Room, at the Police Station, Warrington, on Tuesday morning, respecting the doath of Ernest George Jones, the four year old child of Mr. Arthur Jones. of Liverpool-road, who was killed by the fall of a slab of stone on Slotember It.—The inquest was opened last Monday, but was adjourned, owing to the absence of Mr H. Fairclough, the c-intractor. Mr. Arthur Browne appeared for the father of the deceased, Mr. Stanley Wilson (deputy t )wn clerk) for the Corporation, Mr. Unsworth for Mr. Fairclough, and Mr. FJrshaw for Messrs. Williams and Clay, sub-contractors. Mr. Barton was foreman of the jury. Mr. Unsworth wished to be allowed to explain that one reason why the inquiry was adjourned was because Mr. Fairclough was in Paris. At that time he (the speaker) was under the impression that it was the duty ot Messrs. 'Wi'liams and Clay, ;to take down the stone along with the (Auer slabs which had been removeci,:but Mr. Fairclough had since returned to Warrington, and they now exonerated entirely Mr Clay from any duty to remove this slab of stone. S, far as he was concerned there was an end of the matter.

The Coroner : You say you admit that it was not part of their duty to tak3 the slab down ? Mr. liusworth : We admit that. Proceeding, Mr Unsworth said he had witnesses to call who would des- cribe what took place on the Friday night when the place was left secure, as they thought. The Coroner asked Mr. Wilson what he had to say dbout the matter.
Mr. Wily:in : We rely upon our contract with Mr. Fairclough, and 8%7 we have nothing to do with the matter

The Coroner read the specification for the wcrk, one of th 3 clauses reading as follows :—" The contractor must take all risks of the old and new prope.tty, of life and limbs of workmen, pedestrians, or other persons, and must take proper steps to ensure the safety of such."

Mr. Unsworth : This is a question of criminal nezli- gence. My friend Mr. Wilson rather suggested that they relied upon the c,m3tract to relieve them of any criminal liability, but I submit they cannot do so. The Coroner : Wny ? Suppose I was the owner of certain property and it had to be pulled down and re- erected. I should say " Mr. Unsworth, what will you do it for ?" You say " £500." Very well, we will have a specification and estimate prepared, and I will leave it to you to pull down and re-erect. I then go off to the Continent for a month and leave you in Warrington.You then go to your foreman and say, " Here is a specifica- tion. This is to be done." Your foreman is in full charge, and while he is in full charge this accident happens. It is the foreman I :have to look at and I have to say whether he is criminally responsible; I must go through the story to get at what you have done.— Mr. Unsw,)rth : I am nct suggesting that for a moment ; but carry your suggestion a little further. If you interfere with my work after I have left it-- The Coroner : If I come back from Paris and interfere that is a different thine. Are you going to suggest that the Corporation interfered ? Mr. Unsworth : Yes,
The Coroner : It is quite clear the responsibility of doing certain work is on your client ; and I don't think the Corporation want to say anything more at pre- sent.

Mr. Unsworth said he would call his witnesses. William Hamall, 89, Cartwright-street, said he was in the employ of Mr. Fairclougla as a bricksetter, and he was sent to the place on the Wednesday before the accident. Be had :orders to build a new urinal. A labourer named Elliott took down the old urinal ; witness did nothing with the old place. When the old wall was pulled down he noticed the slab. It had stood there from the Wednesday to the Friday night. when they left it by itself. There was a pipe " cased up round it." Mr Unsworth : The pipe was fastenecl to the slab. Witness : Yes, and the pipe was enclosed in a wooden casing which was secured to the slab by four bolts.

A. wooden model of tbe place, prepared by Mr. Clay, junior was handed to the Coroner. Continuing, witness said that on Friday he tested the slab as to its firmness. It was tested as it stood by itself on Friday at six o'clock. It was 6.10 when the men left the place. He and another man pw.hed each side a great deal hard2r than any child could have pushed. _ _

The Coroner : Are you going' to allege that the Cor- poration took the casing away ? Mr. Unsworth : Yes, sir, and interferel with the ground. The Coroner If he says that at the time he left it the flig was sate that is sufficient for your purpose. The witness says that he and another man pushed on both sides, and it stood there, and that there was a pipe standing up with a casting around. (To the witness : ) Did von leave the job at 6.10 on Friday? Witness : Yes, sir. The Coruner : And in your opinin it was safe? Witness : Quite.

In answer to Mr.Browne.witness said the pipe alluded to was only a half-inch lead pipe. There was a casing round the pine. The casing went into the ground. The Corooer : As a matter of fact the slab was safe on the Friaay night. It was quite safe when the men left. I would lihe this witness to tell me what it was proposed to do with the slab supposing the Corporation never touched it. If the slab bad not fallen wbat was to be done ?

Witness: I have no idea. The Coroner • Had Mr Fairclough any obligation on him to do anything with it? Witness: I cannot say. The Ceroner : When was the pipa removed ? Mr Unsworth : We suggest it was removed on the Saturday morning. The Coroner: Without any notice to you. Mr Unsworth : _ Yes, sir.
_ The Coroner: Do you mean to say that between the removal of the pipe and the accident you had no notice the pipe had gone? Mr Unmoral : None whatever.

The Coroner : At six o'clock on Friday night, I understand,Mr Fairclough's trim bad done as much work askthey possibly could. They could not use the slab mita the water pipe was taken away. This man on his oath says that 1...9 and another man tested the slab to ascertaisa whether it •••22 perfectly safe or otherwise. The question arose why the Corporation took away the only support this stone had, and left it standing there in four inches of soil.

Mr Browne (to witness) : Why did you:test the Witness : Because we were leaving the job. The Coroner: It never came down until tbe Corpora- tion took away the support. What can the Corporation say in answer to that ? The Deputy Town 'Jerk : I have only just heard of this. I have sent up for the person who gave instruc- tions for this pipe to be removed. In answer to Mr Unswortb, witness said there were some surf ace flags against the slab,which were a support to it.

The Coroner said that if the Corporation took away the water service pipe that was running by the slat:lo.nd in doing so removed one of the surface flags, he did not see where Mr Fairclougt's liability came in. . .

James Carradice, a bricksetter in Mr Fairclough's employ, said he was on the work in company with the last witness. They tried the flag on the Friday night and used a fair amouet of force. No child could have knockei it down.
The Coroner: In your opinTon it was safe to leave it as it was?

Witness: Perfectly safe. Continning, he said there was a surface pipe rucning alongside the slab. This was cased round, and was bolted through the flag. The Coroner: Anyone wanting to disconnect the pipe would have to take away one of the flags ? Witness: Yee. They would require to take up a portion of the floor of the old urinal to get the pipe away William Johnson, 14 Miner-street, employed at Messrs. Crosfleld's Works, said he frequentls saw the work in question going on. On Saturday morning, about seven o clock, on going to his work he Fa w a man working with a spade near the slab of stone which after wards fell. On asking him what he was doing he said he was going to remove a p'pe. When witness came blok he saw a man working at the pipe and in the act of remov• lug two staples that held it to the slab of;stone. The Coroner: Had they taken away any of the stones that formed the fl)or of the old vrinal to get at tha pipe? _

Witness: I could not say, but one man was using a I spade and another was :loosening she pipe from the stone. Replying to a further question from the Coroner, witness said it was impossible to disconnect the pipe without taking the flag away. The man who was dig- ging was a Corporation labourer. Tha Deputy Town Clcrk asked what the man was doing. Witness said he was disturbing the ground when be saw them in the first instance. He had got down a few inches. Witness did not think that they could get hold of the pipe and rip it up. The wall that was taken down had not been a support to the slab for a consider— able length of lime. The Deputy Town Clerk contended that Mr. Fair- dough's men ought to have taken down the slab. The Coroner : They could not take it down because the Corporation had not removed the water pipe. The Corporation men came on Saturday morning,and it must be apparent to any sensible man that they made the stone no more secure, but more insecure. They ought to have supported it.

The Deputy Town Clerk: The Corporation had nothing whatever to do with it. A Juror: lithe Corporation had not done that work for a week the stone would have been standing yet. • The Coroner : Exactly. Most likely it would have been standing now and would never have come down if the Corporation had not interfered. Why did they not go to the contractor immediately they removed the pipe and inform him of the fact?
Mr, Unswottn (to witness) : Was it possible to tip

THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, SEPTEMBER 14, 190 G WARRINGTON ASSESS- MENTS.

Appeals by Licensed Victuallers. A Eneetng ot the Warrington Union Assessment Com- mittee was held in the Board Room at the Workhouse on Friday. Mr. George Pilling presided, and there were also present :—Messrs A J Jolley, William Houghton. William Hickman, J Billinge, A Jolley, T Halton, S Davies, J Johnson, J Clarke, E L Bent, and J C Sutton (clerk), S Sutton (assistant clerk), William Owen (valuer), W H Woodcock (assistant overseer).
THE SAVINGS BANE ASSESSMENT..

Mr Thomas TIINSTALL appealed against the increase of the assessment of the Warrington Savings Bank, by £l7. He pointed out that the assessment of the residence in connection with the bank had been decreased by £ll so that th.l total increase cas £6. The trustees felt that instead of there being an increase there should be a decrease. The CLERK ; All who appeal think that. (Laughter.) Mr WOODCOCK said the assessment was raised to the round sum of £lOO because the overseers thought the bank was worth that amount. Mr TIINSTALL said property had materially decreased in value in the vicinity of the bank. It was decided to reduce the assessment to the former figure.

div.head: PUBLIC -HOUSE APPEALS.
div.p: PUBLIC -HOUSE APPEALS.

Mr. ARTHUR BROW-NE—on behalf of Mrs Loy, the Licensee of the Eagle and Child Inn, appealed against the increased assessment of the house which now stood at £lOO gross and £76 103 rateable. Mr Browne pointed out that the house was situated at the back of Bridge. street and did no morning trade at all. Sometimes Mrs Loy did not take two shillings all morning. The greatest takings in a single week amounted to £l6 and the loweat Lll. The average takings were £l3 103 per week. Never more than two barrels had been sold In a single week. The stables were a loss to her and the sale yard brought very little extra custom to the house, because as soon as tbe sales-were over the people proceeded to the Norton Arms. Mr. BICH:HAN : Could you say what the rent of the sale-yard is ? Mr. HOUGHTON said at the Norton Arms it was £25 a year and more business was dons there. Mr. JOLLEY : The mill in connectioa with the Eagle and Child is now empty. Mr. WOODC:CIC : What rent does she pay? Mr. BROWNE : £65. Mr. WOODCOCK : it has been assessed in the same ratio as the rest of the public-houses. The CHAIRIItN said the house would be a very good one when it was brought to the front but at present it was a poor one. He felt certain that the licensee was hardly making a living at the place. ' It was decided to reduce the aSsessment to £BO gross and £6B rateable, the same as before tie reassessment. Mr, BROWNE then appealed on behalf of John Lockett, holder of an outdoor beer licence in Lythgoes-lane, known as Providence Place, against his increased assessment. Mr Browne said it was busy assessed at £34 rateable and was formerly £25 10s. Mr Lockett did not sell more than five barrels a fortnight. The house belonged to the Empress Brewery Conapany of Old Trafford, and Mr Lockett did not make more than 8s or 10s a week. .
Mr WOODCOCK: Doesn't he carry on a business there as well ? . . _ ..
_ Mr Baowxs : There is a small greengrocery business.

Mr WOODCOCK said the overseers raised the assessment to the value placed upon it by the Inland Revenue authorities, and that was £4O, which value bad been paid on for the last seven years to the Inland Revenue authorities. Mr 13110WNE : The landlord has paid the income tax. Mr A J JOLLEY considered the fizure a very moderate one an', proposed that it remain as at present. Mr. HALTON said from th. fizures Riven, the licensee I was selling more b3er than Mrs. Loy at the Eagle and Child.

It was decided to let the assessment stand as at present. Mr. BROWNE appealed against the inlreased assessment of the off-licensed housq in Thelwall Lane, in charge of John Lythgoe. Be stated that the road in which the house was situated was not a thoroughfare and there were only 31 houses which the licensee could serve. The rent was £lB a year and the house belonged to the Empress Brewery Company, Old Trafford. The licensee had never sold more than six barrels of beer per month for th,,, last six years. Mr. A. J. jOLLEY said there was a footpath over the locks which would enable people to reach this holm.

Mr. BROWNE said his client did not serve anyone on the opposite side of the locks. Mr. WOODCOCK said the asseqsment had been raised from £2O to £29. In adding £9 the overseers had only made a reasonable increase. 'There was no evidence that the rent had been reduced.
Mr. BilowNE : When the Ship C tnal was being made the lieens,?e sold six barrels a week. Mr. A J. JOLLEY : You didn't ask for the assessments to be raised. - - -

It was decided to let the assesqn3ent remain as fixed. WiLuard ASPINALL, of the Railway Inn, appealed against the inereased aosessment of his house to £BO gross and £65 rat-able. He statPr3 th4t his rent had been recently reduced from £BO to £7O. The trade at the house was not so good as it had been. Mr. WOODCOCK: We have only added £lO to the rent.
Mr. HALTON saiithe trade had gone off very much indeed at this house. _ _ _ _
Mr. BILLINGE proposed that it be reduced to £65 gross And £55 rateable. Mr. A JOLLEY seconded. . _ .

Mr". A J JOLLEY said on the evidence there was no justification for reducing the assessment. There was no evidence beyond the bare statement that the hJuse was not doing as much business as before. When Vie busi- ness increased,the licensees did not voluntarily tell them of it. He moved fan amendment that the assessment remain. Mr HICKMAN seconded. _ .

On a vote being taken, Mr Billinge's resolution was carried and the assessment was accordingly reduced to £65 gross and £55 rateable. THOMAS Caorarrox, the licensee of the Blackburn Arms, Market Place, appealed against the increased assessment of his premises. Be said that the chief business of the Market bad now been removed to the other end, away from his house, and the result was that the business was not as good as it used to be. In fact on a Saturday the business was net better than it used to be on a Wednesday. The sale of beer had consider- ably reduced. The rent was £lOO per annum. Mr. Woodcock menticned that the assessment had been increasad from £1.15 to £l5O. It was considered from the business which Mr Crompton did at his house that the assessment ought to be considerably more than that fixed by the overseers. The committee decided to allow the assessment to re- main.

div.head: ASSESSMENT OF THE BORAX WORKS,
div.p: THE ASSESSMENT OF THE BORAX WORKS,

Mr. E.ll. FLEMING appealed on behalf of Messrs. Bishop and Company agailsat the increased assessment of their borax works off Dial-street. Be said the only question he wished to put before them was that for two years their works had been more or less idle on account of the stoppage of raw material and at the present time the works were entirely closed. The firm were making arrangements for obtaining raw material which they hoped would not prolong the stoppage of the works for more than a year. They therefore asked for the clemency of the committee during that time. Mr WILLIAM OWEN eaid that on account of the partial stoppage of the works the assessment had been reduced to £204 gross and £lB6 rateable. It was decided that Mr. Owen should report further to the committee on the matter. THE VALUERS REPORT.

Hearing that Mr. A. H. Crosfield, an Englishman who is a member of the Hoylake and St. Andrew's Golf Clubs and takes a keen interest in. the game, was paying a visit to Chicago, our representative enquired whether there was any chance of an Eng- lish team of golfers coming out this fall. "Well," replied Mr Crosfield, " I am afraid not. Mr Ryder Richardson, our energetic secretary at Hoylake, has tried to push the thing forward and Mr R Peters told me the other day in Newport that he had sounded some of the leading Scotch players at St. Andrews. Nothing,however,has come of this so far: more's the pity I think. You've now, added Mr Crosfield; talent in America,both amateur and professional, which would make our best amateurs look to their laurels. On the other hand, experience counts for so much that I am convinced a visit of our most accomplished golfers would tend to raise the average standard of play here Anyhow having tried conclusions at so many other games, it`does seem anomalous to leave out golf,the prince of them all, as Mr. A J Balfour justly calls it.,, Is it not about time we had some test matches arranged ?—"As aforesaid, I think the rising school of golfers out here would be able to pick up a wrinkle or two from our classical performers." You mean, for instance? "Well at St. Andrews they will tell you Mr. Leslie Balfour-Melville has the most correct and orthodox style, or rather what approaches nearest to that intangible ideal. Be is a must persistent and determined player and I have a vivid recollec- tion of seeing him a few years since lower Mr John Ball junes. colours in the final round of the amateur championship at St. Andrews. There has seldom been so popular a win,unless one is to site the many victories of Johnny Ball himself. Then there is Mr. Laidlay, the hero of a hundrel fights, one of Scotland's greatest champions. I suppose no one, not even Taylor, has a greater mastery of the iron ; assuredly no one has a greater power of concentra- tion on the game." You think it needs absorption? "Well, apropos of that, yon know the tale of an Pnglish lady watching:some golf in Scotland. As the French say English people take their pleasures sadly, so she exclaimed at the serious way in which the Scotch people were treating the game. Hoot Madam' came the reply with marked disapproval from some didactic Northern bystander Hets na a game at a', bets jist the study o' a life time.' Mr Laidlay has made a study of it,and to great purpose., He settles down to his work in earnest, and in his own peculiar style of " forward " play. As Horace Hutchinson remarks, in that style Mr Laidlay has many disciples, but no equal." Replying to a remark that Mr Hutchinson from his literary skill is better known in America than any other English golfer, Mr. Crosfield said, "I can assure you that his golf ie as polished as his writing. Finished and artistic in every department of the game Mr. Hut- chinson's prettiest shot is the approach played with the old fashioned baffy spoon. Indeed with pos- sibly the single exception of Mr. Hilton, he has probably command of the most subtle executlon with the wooden club. Hutchinson is no sign-post. "Then cake Allan Macfte,an ex-amateur champion like those I have mentioned above. Lacking only distance, Mr !stadia is par excellence the golfer of consistent clock-work accuracy. Like Mrs Battle,a stickler for the rigor of the game and entertaining the supromest contempt for pot hunting and pot hunters (that he won a prize I gave at Cannes was the merest accident and much against his will) he is possessed of a wit as keen and quick as the snap of his übiquitous kodak. Mr J Low is another great proficient at the game and like Mactie his shrewd sense of humour Iwould in itself finally refute Sydney Smith's delicious libel on Scotchmen," _

You mean his remark that it required a surgical operation to get a joke into a Scotch man's head? Yes, and his further observation that their only idea of wit north of the border, or that inferior variety which under the name of wit was so infi- nitely distressing to people of taste, consisted in immodetete laughter at stated iteervals. Our genial friends, Sir Mitchell Banks, George Dunlop and others make us proud in Liverpool circles of our after-dinner oratory when golfers foregather." "Johnny Low's style is different, but about his Postprandial efforts, there is positively a flavor of eighteenth century genius. His golf is A-I,and his performances with the wooden putter approach the miraculous; but his tales are hest of all." "The Hon. H. H. Finche-Batton is the only prominent golfer I know—a very dashing player too —who can rival J. bow as raconteur. You ask, about Mr. Ferguson? Yes,of course Mare Ferguson is in the very front rank and a team coming out here would not be complete without him. The feature of his game is his exceptional power in playing pushed half-shots, which if it were not an Irishism, I should call full half-shots, Another feature is a sort of bull-dog tenacity.which perhaps partially accounts for the faculty Mr. Ferguson has, at a pinch, for holing out puts that are not quite dead. I doubt, however, if any golfer is more reli- able or consistent in holing out four to six foot puts than Lord Winchilsea who played so finely and successfully in the amateur championship at Sand- wich this year." "You have heard of course of Mr Ted Blackwell and his phenomenal drives. They tell me I shall , see here at Chicago the longest driver in the world." . .

You think that— a touch"of the American taste for superlatives ? (Mr Crostield, laughing) "Well, no! but on one or two points lam sceptical. It would be almost easier to conceive of Jack Roberts being beaten at English billiards than of Mr Blackwell being out- driven by mortal man at golf, on a calm day that is or down wind. Braid (whose style is modelled on that of Douglas Roland) hits a terrific low " wind cheater" and I am not sure that Blackwell's soar- ing ball would travel as far in the teeth of a gale. Certainly it was worth going to St Andrews this summer, if for nothing else than to see Braid hit the

_ A FABLE. —A wine merchant left a suspected assistant in his cellar, and said to him, "Now, lest you should drink the wine while I am away, I will chalk your mouth, so that I may know it." He then rubbed his nail across the man's lips, and pretented to leave the mark of chalk on them. The man drank of the wine, and chalked his mouth, and thus discovered himself.

What on earth gave you such an idea?" Mr. Wheeler (desperately): "That is the only way I can account for the number of pedals I barked my shins against in the dark just now."

NEW YORK, WEDNESDAY.

All attempts at burying the dead at Galves- ton have been abandoned. Yesterday hundreds of bodies were taken out to sea and thrown overboard. No efforts have been neglected to prevent a pestilence. The sick and injured are receiving all attention, bat the physicians fear that many will die owing to the impossibility of affording them air. Every able-b3died man is engaged in the work of relief. Little stealing was reported yesterday, and there were also no murders. Some 50 marauders have been shot for robbing the dead.

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS.
Mr. Kruger's Flight. Arrival at Lourenco Marques.

LOURENCO MARQUES, WEDNESDAY, 10.35 A.M. Mr. Kruger reached here by special train. An engine ran through to here:from Komati Poort and returned with two empty passenger carriages. Tbis unusual proceeding aroused suspicion,and the denouement followed when Mr. Kruger, Mr. Reitz, and other officials turned up at exactly 9.30 o'clock last night. The train was stopped at a siding outside the town.
It appears that ex-President Steyn was left behind, as he is very sick.
The International Law on
the Question of Capture.

A representative of the Press Association en Wednesday conveyed to Mr. John Westlake, Q.C., an authority on international law, the news of the flight of Mr. Kruger to Lourenco Marques, with the object of ascertaining that gentleman's opinion as to the position of the ex-President of the South African Republic. "I am very glad to hear the news," said Mr. Westlake, "Kruger is now perfectly safe from the hands of the British. There is no possible way we can get him—no, no possible way. I am glad to say be is safe. It relieves us of a great responsibility. It gets rid of what might have been a very troublesome matter, and he can do no harm to us wherever he goes. He may remain on Portuguese territory as long as be likes without fear of the British, or he may go where be likes on a neutral ship. Yes,he is quite free from us now. We cannot touch him."

div.head: With the Warrington Volunteers.
div.p: With the Warrington Volunteers.
Another Letter from Captain Appleton.
The Mayor has reclived the followinz letter from Captain Appleton, who commands the Warrington vol- unteers in South Africa._
Gras Kop, near Sandepruit, Auzuet 3rd, 1900.

_ Dear Mr. Roberts, I received your long interesting letter last mail and I need not say how delighted I was to receive it, and to bear all the Warrington news which it contained. I read the letter to my Company and they were most interested in it and we are all most grateful to you for your continued and unabated inter ost in our doings and in our welfare, and for all your kind mes- sages to us. I wrote to you last from Leuwspruit and I think you pretty well know our movements up to that place. We remained there until July 15th, when our detachment under Major Adam was ordered four miles nearer Standerton to Kroindraai station, where we had the station itself, two culverts, a level crossing and about two miles of railway under our cerreWe had a bee kopje or rather rise of ground about half a mile eouth of camp which we entrenched arid upon which we spent a good deal of hard work with pick and Orme. We had a naval 12 pounder gun there and also a floe dummy gun consieting of a long tubular steel signal poet from the Railway Station which Msj ,r Adam commandeered and mounted lo a gun pit. Tai bore a very strong resemblance to a 4 7 naval gun at quite a short distance and we 'flattered ourselvoe that we deceived Brother Boer. Major Adam was again complimented upon his trenches and defences by the General who came over to inspect and had lunch in our mess. We had a good many farms round us in some of which were Boers who had surrendered and in many of which the wives and children were left while the farmer was away on commando; these people all required careful watching and some of the ladies gave a good deal of trouble with letters demanding all sorts of things and they many of them tried to get all the information they could doubtless with a view to sending it on to the "Commando, we had to pot a guard on our nearest neighbours. We were constantly having small expeditions to farms near, and as my company! went out upon one which proved a little exciting I think perhaps a description of it may interest you. A certain large farmer having surrendered and taken the oaths of neutrality was sent back to live and remain upon his farm which is the usual course followed in the first instance if the farmer has not played too censpicuous a part in the war. The Boers descended upon him and carried him off to gaol at Erinelo where he said he was confined with Saffirs and fed upon their fare which seemed to rankle a good deal in his breast. He was then sent cut with one Beer as guard to join Commands again, but he managed to escape and after wandering about the Veldt eventually reached our lines. He asked for an escort to go with him to his farm and buy his stock te prevent it falling into the hands of the Boers. On Friday July 27th a small expedi- tion was despatched under Major Adam and consieed of a squadron of Bethune's Mounted Infantry two (15 lb.) field guns and our company of Infantry with six mule wagons, 10 mules par wagon which beats our Queen, with eight horses to bring back the mollies, &c. in. We left camp at 7.30 a.m. my men and Lieutenant Lewis riding in the waibns and myself on a mount borrowed for the occasion. The farm was nine miles north east of us and upon the Vaal River. The reconnoi- tred to the front and flanks and we reached the farm about 11 o'clock, having left the guns and wagons on an eminence about one mile in rear of firm. The farm was the prettiest I had seen and the house built of stone with trees round and in front of it, and white and blue sweet violets and pansies in bloom Ira the garden. We were regaled on:ham and eggs and tea soon after we arrived. The house was on the slope of a hill and in • front of it was a flat mealie field about 200 yards across; and then the river, which here flowed in a deep wide bed which had to be carefully searched by my patrol while the company extended in front of the farm. On the opposite bank was a kopje with a nasty donga to the left. About 12 o'clock while posting a man on the look out post under Corporal Howard I was returning to the farm across the field when I heard the crack of Vanes rs behind me on the kopje and new our men under Lswis and 8.M.1. tnakiny for the available cover round The farm and ieplying most vigorously to the Beers win) had le'non spotted by my look out man through me glasses (Private Hughes). When I reached the term I found the men all highly delighted and excited at getting a shot nt the enemy who were then abeut 1,000 yards away and abou 50 in number (viaible). In a very few miral ee the first shell from our guns screamed over our heads wh'ich was quickly followed by ethers and some excellently aimed shrapnel which kn leked at least two Boors ever while they and their comrades wore on their horses, and g ;Hoping in open order arid in zio?.z tg fashion for all they were worth to t:et nu': of range. The earn went out, cross d the river, and erezed the kopje and opened fire from there upon the Boers who TeOW spread out and tried to get round our flanks. They leld the kopj ur'tii some of our ny•n hal oaded up the wagons and th, remainder of us had eetended to the left and laid down to watch cur left flank. The Beers were now working round to eet on some kopj,,r weber to our left front and N.ljor Adam rent the Iremainder of the B.M 1. to seize them finest which thee soon did and we heard them exchanging shots with th enemy at a lone range. As soon as our wagons were , ready to start they were sent on in front end we all retire d, try company and some of the B.M I esc-rine them and the guns while the remainder held the kepje3 en our flanks and rear in succession as we retired. After a desultory firine in rear we al; reached camp safely atout 6 p.m. happily without any castle Ries.

We had a huge drove of oxen and about 50 fiae white turkeys and meliies and butter, etc. Tois was a nice little object lesson on of course a very small scale of the extreme mobility of the 13)ers and proved how very necessary it is to have mounted trop a and guns with Infantry in opposing them. Tney had evidently not been informed of the guns which hai not been spotted among the wagons or they would not have come so close to us and but for them would probably have come a good deal closer and the result would have been I fear some casualties on our side.

The farmer who gave us some interestieg accounts cf the war from the Boer side and who told us there were Hippopotami in the river some eight years ago or Sea Cows as he called them, spent the night in our camp and then went ;in to Plat- rand to live under our protection while his wife an Idaughter remained to take care of the farm. We did not care much for the gentleman %leo was far too English all of a midden (as many of them ire) and who spoke far too much against his own people. Another morning just a couple of days before leaving Kromdraai while we were digging we saw about 50 Boers coming over the sky line and driving in our mounted scouts. We all manned the trenches and had one shot at them from the naval 12 pounder, which soon scattered them, and they all went back over the skyline with the exception of one scout. The gun got the range splendidly at 7,500 yards but a little too much to their right. On August Lt we got an order at 11.30 a.m. to move by the afternoon train to Sandspruit and so we struck camp at 1.30 a.m. but the train did not arrive until nearly 4 o'clock when we stormed some huge open iron trucks which we found a bit chilly befote we reached Sandspruit at 7 p.m. in a eharp frost. The contents )1 our truck were rather assorted—about 50 N.C.Ohs and men, firewood, mess stores, corrugated iron sheets (most useful for shelters and kitchens) turkeys, hens, rations, six officers and the officer commanding detachment seated on a long and rather shaky throne of firewood. It was a bad time for men with large feet as the floor space was pretty well covered with our live stock. We pitched camp by moonlight, about a mile north of the station and at ab3ut 9.30 a.m, next morning started for this mountain. Gras Kep six to seven miles away to the north. We are in a most charming position here 6,000 feet above sea level with a magnificent view of veldt and mountain for at least 20 miles round and in the afternoon from about four o'clock to sunset everything stands out very clearly and it is a grand time for observ- ing the enemy, A Boer picquet, Amersfront and the Boer Lager near it (12 miles away) are distinctly visihle through glasses. The view of Majeba is als ) very flue , with its steep side and flit top and you will find the sketch* at the head of this letter by a Private in H Company and which w!ll amuse you, gives you a very good idea of its shape Which is doubtless already familiar to you. This hill has been splendidly entrenched by the rT)rsqs whom we relieved and has three tiers of trenches and the top which rises to three conical points is a regular keep and coveted with trenches and gun pits. It is a large mountein with long stretches of grass on the higher part below the keep. All our Companies are in detached camps and form little commandos of their own with their own trenches and our 4th Company is on another spur of the mountain two miles away a,alied Arnold Hill. We have construeted a splendid mess shelter sunk about two feA down and walled with biscuit Loxes and roofed with corrugated iron. We all like the place immensely and the air is splendid hut o course we have wind and mist, the latter only occasi ally in the early morning so far. We have Some perfec days. sunny and not too hot. Major Adam shot a buck yesterday morning with a rifle belonging to Private Fearrhey of my Company and who helped to carry the spoil home and is to have a hind quarter to himself. The Major went out again to day with Lewis and a covering party from my Company about two miles out and stalked some spring bok but could not get near enough to them on account of the wind changing and carrying the scent of the sportsmen. He got three shots and one was pretty close. They however startled a Baer scout on watch behind a low kopjo on their left but did not get a shot at him. He galloped away quickly. I fear lam spinning a very long yarn and must not weary you. I forget whether I told you in my previous letter of all the wanton wreckage of houses and propeety in Natal. The Boer farms here contain a lot of furniture looted from the Natal people and b lock at some of the houses and railway stations in Natal you would say that savages and not Christians had been there. Of course nearly every railway bridge and culvert was blown up which is quite legitimate warfare bet you cannot wonder at the Natal Meonted Troops feeling pretty mad end in clined to reciprocate a little when they get the chacce. SUNDAY AUGUST STH.—To-Jay there is a beautiful warm sun(noe too hot) and cool breeze. We all bad to turn out last night at 8 o'clock owing to some firing having been heard on the North side of the hill which turned out afterwards to have been s'nota fired from one of our trenches at some wandering sheep so the garrison retired to bed in safety. We had General Lyttleton and his Staff on the mountain yesterday r.cminoitri,l7, for , an advance in force this week of which we ought to have a grand view from here and which will be ancient -history long before this letter reaches you. I am glad to hear that we shall return to the 'County of Warrington.' We were very sorry to bear of the deaths in the town. I knew Mr. Dennis Davies well by sight and had vny much enjoyed his acting. He teak after hi 3 father in this respect. His death is very sad indeed. I sincerely hope we may also find you in office for a second year on our return which I hope will be this side of Caristmas. I fear things are very bad in China, but oar latest news is that the legations are still safe though besieged. We were also much shocked to hoar of the ell fear), painful death of the Duke of Edinburgh and of the brutal assassinatioa of the King of Italy. The world is lull of horrors just now. I wish I could have you here for an hour or two to see the magnificent view of the Drakeaaberg and other moun- tains, but I think you would find a short stay in the country quite enough. • With many thanks for your letter and its messages to I us, and kindest best remembrances from us all to you and all Warrington friends.—Believe me, yours sincerely, F. M. APPLETON. P.S.—My men are busy cutting up and skinning goats which often stray up on to the mountain. I tear the meat will be very fresh, but they will not keep it. MONDAY AUGUST 6 —To-city is very windy and makes things rather uncomfortable. I met my sponge on a journey a long way off my tent and some of the man's things took a trip to the bottom of the hill. I lent your letter to some of the Warrington men in our detachment who would I know be much interested in reading it. I knew several of them Sergeant Price (signalling sergeant) Corporal Mellor, and Private Lea (H Company). We always cot Warrington papers each week and as you imagine they are eagerly read. My Colour Sergeant (Sergeant Killen) has nad a sad trouble to bear in the loss of his wife at Newton where be lived as Sergeant Instructor to our Newton Company. AUGUST 7.—We had rather an interesting day to-day and so lam inflict:ug you still further. Our advance on Amersfront from Pardekep took place to-day and the atmosphere was abnormally clear even far South Africa so we had a grand view but a crual wind. There was very heavy shelling on 13)th sides and we could see the Atolls bursting very clearly and the Boers retir- ing, and they lighted grass fires as usual to cover their retreat. We bad evidently driven them off Bleu Kop and must now hold Amersf rent. I fear a good many Boers got away, we saw thcir wagons and (probably guns) making off cowards the south east (Wakkeretro mountains) and Major Adam telegraphed their position ,at once, and heliographed as soon as he could get connection, and so I hope our cavalry got at them,but I fear it is doubtful.

A krge quaatity of presents from Warrington have at last arrived and we are 1.17,-311in" in all the good things* I have no chubt that Uonel Hall will have acknow- ledged them but I may venture to thank you and all the kind donors in Warring'on and District on behalf of my• self and my Company and if you could see how they havo been received you ~vonld Lave no doubt as to the way they are apprecia'el W all look quite re9pectable again. The nighta are in st beautiful (good moon at present) The Warrington field glasse!, and especially my own have been in use all day and wo always hava one going in each trench every dig MO they are w mderfully use- ful .ar night when there is a rnQon. . . . .

Ths s"ketch referred to is Chambßrla;n and Kruger in boxing costume; the Union Jack being round Chamber- lain and the Transvaal Colours round Kruger with Nl3juba Hill as the boxing ground. Chanabarlain is just giving Kruger the " Knock-out " blow.]

The authorities have changed their minds with regard to retaining the services of the whale of the militia during the autumn and winter and are aseertainiag the feeling of officers and men as to the disembodiment of certain battalions before the advent of winter. It assembled at its headquarters at Warrington on 22nd of last January, and is now in Ireland where alsa the 6th Battalion is likewise located.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football.
[By " OvaUsti

There was no end of exuberant joy in Warrington on Saturday evening, for the local team bad in the afternoon managed to put " paid" to Salford's account and the circumstances naturally afforded much happi- ness. Last season the boot was on the other leg. Somehow or other the Manche3ter clubs always get heartily welcomed at Warrington, and they never fail to meet with a burning desire on the part of the locals to bring about their downfall. This is part of the welcome. With the single exception of Oldham or Swinton there is no team that Warrington are so keen on taking down as Salford. To spill the gore of the Reds is the one thing wanted te complete Warrington's nappiness, and on Saturday they spilled quite a lot of it —meta- phorically speaking of course.

Both teams had won all their previous en.gagments— one each—and were therefore mimed with any amount of cznOdence in themselves. The Reds were particu- larly cheerful on arrival, for had they not got a forward team that would make mincemeat of Warrington in the twinkling of an eye? Of course they had, but the meat for mincing proved rather rough. Oh ! it was a struggle, and at times you could not tell where primrose and blue ended and red blgan.

The day was nice and warm too, which wag I think. a factor in the home team's victory. Some of the Salfordians were net in a state of health to relish hard work under a summer sun. They were in a melting mood and the melting process was not quite as comfort- able as that in a rurkish Bath, though uquilly effeqive. There has been some undieguisPd crowhg in New Barns neighbourhool this last fortnight about Salforces fine forwards. And the' are fine—fine animals. I never saw finer porkers at the Christmas show in town. There's plenty of meat about the" belles of New Barns" and tor a time tbis superabundance of meat looked like overwhelming Warrington.

During the whole of the first quarter the visitors had the upper hand, and the way they won the scrimmages boded ill for the home tam's chances. But the pace was a cracker, and in the end bone and muscle triuniped over avoirdupois. Once the Warringtou men got the measure of their opponents and they proceeded to run them off their feet—And did it too. Salford lost their best. chance after the first quarter, and Warrington opened the scoring with a goal from Fish. Then a sprint by the Reds put them 3 point ii front.for Aldred and Shaw got a try and a anal betwben them. Warring- ton retaliated with interest, Mereweather and Fish following snit, and the interval came with the score 7 points to 5 in favour of Warrington.

The second half was practically a repetition of the first, with Warrington a bit the stronger all round. Hockenhall added another try in very neat style, and Salford act a dropped goal. It was a ding-dong sttuggle and the issue was ewr in doubt, for the speedy back 3 of the visitors often looked like equalising. Play was of an exceptionally high order, and when Warrins.ton re- tire] victors by 10 pins to 7 points, tho home crowd opined it had seen something worth its money—and it had.

There was some brilliant individual play on both sides, Fish and Hallam on the home side performing wonders, the one on the attack and the other on the defence. Two of Fish's runs during the day were magnificent, and he fully deserved a try in addition to the two goals he kicked. Isherwood started very un- steadily but showed some of his old form towards the close, while Lawless and Hockenhall combined very well on the right. At half-back Warrington were a bit over- shadowed by Grey and Griffiths, who were the cleverer pair. For hard work however Burgess and Duckworth could not have been beaten, and they gave a better passing display than at Widnes. The forwards played a marvellous game and practically ran the heavier Salford men to a standstill. Mereweather and Board- man were always on the ball or the man, and the latter's speed seems to have improved since last season. Altogether Warrington's display was such as to heartily satisfy the la nne spectators who are expecting great things this season.

Dan Smith was the best man for the visitors, and but for his sterling play at full back they must have had a heavier :margin azainst them. Williams and Pearson also played well, but Crocker was a failure, and Aldred allowed himself to be run in touch too often. Beyond speed, there does not seem to be very much in the ex- Tyldesley threequarter.

The Warrington lads have done as I exhorted them— honoured the new flag—and the committee have bon- 61urel the players and spectators by providing the men with a new outfit in jersey's. They looked better than at Widnes by a lot.
By the way the crowd was of such dimensions as to make a happy augury for the future. Over £9O was taken at the gate and Treasurer Pemberton now smiles the smile of the man whose coffers are filling.

Runcorn had the misfortune to visit Swinton with Houghton, Butterworth, and Faulkner absentees, and the Blues took the opportunity of avenging themselveg for las: season's defeat. They ran up a score of 17 plias to nil. Oldham found Barrow a bard nut to crack as the score of two tries to one shows. St. Helens had not much trouble in defeating Rochdale Hornets, and as they also have won their opening matches, the contest between Warrington and St. Helens at Wilders- p)ol to-day should be a good one.

For this match Warrington are relying on exactly the same team as last week, Bate not having yet played himself into form. They ought to manage the Saints easily enough: and avenge last season's heavy defeat. If St. Helens are satisfactorily accounted for Warrington will not only have won: the three opening matches, bat they will have gained a clear 6 points on the corres- ponding games last season.

Fletcher Russell's have opened their home season in capital style by defeating Stockport " A" on Saturday, the margin of two tries to nil being a comfortable one. Stockport played pluckily and thegame was contested in a thoroughly friendly spirit on either side. Tom Knight was very safe at back whilst J W Clare (who by the way has only played in less than half a donn games) fairly took the eye of the spectators. Foden at half was Moo very good and the forwards who are a sturdy lot will cause trouble to future opponents.

To-day (Saturday) Wines" A" are the visitors to the Wellfiald-street ground and with ordinary good fortune should be accounted for, which will go far to encourage the homestnrs in their games with Oldham " A" at Warrineton on the 22nd and Salford " A " at Salford on the 29th instant. It is intere9ting to note that the great- est unanimity exists between the officials of the Club and the players and this together with the enthusiasm prevailing :irnongst thl tiam should be very encourag - leg to Secretary filinbridge and his co-workers. What is now needed is a little public support, in the shape of spectators.

In our columns we publish a statement of the finan cial position of Runcorn R ural Council for the balf-year ended March 31st last. The accounts were duly audited a week ago. The half-year was commenced with a balance of £4,390 us in and them was received from the rates £3,010 for general expenses and £725 183 10d for special expenses, a total call upon We ratepayers of £3,735 18s 10 I. In the previous half year of 1899 the ratepayers contributed £4,252 9s 11d. The grant under the. Agri- cultural Rates Act was £445 14s, and the Cheshire County Council paid £l7O towards the salaries of the medical officer and the inspector of nuisances. Water rates produced £338 3s id. and other small items brought up the total on th e receipt side to £9,208 Os 4d Tile payments included £3. 796 33 81 for high ways, of which £3,283 13.1 101 was for maintenance and .repair of roads other than main roads,and 5:347 lla for repayment and interest of loans and £l4l 18s 7d for salaries of officers. Sewerage works cnst £ll4 11s sd; waterworks £205 9i 6 public lighting, £l3O 16s id; scavenging £66 1. Od; repayment of principal and interest on loans, £540 163 lid ; salaries of officers, £314 93 sd, and establishment charges £l3l 7s Si. Opposition to the London and North- Western Railway Co., cost £3O. There are investments to the amount of £5OO The payments totalled £6,C92 103 3d,leaving a balance in band of £3,115 10t le.

It was a difficult matter to thoronghly understand the Clerk's statement. The CLERK said it was impossible to give such a statement in submitting estimated expenditure only. Mr. KNOWLES : Let him come and look through the books. It will be a little entertainment for him. (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN pointed out that the estimates were charges up on the common funds of the Union, and he understood that Mr. Forshaw desired a statt-meat show- ing the amount received from the several townships and the amount expended on the same' The CLERK said there were certain country parishes which had very few paupers but still they paid a large amount to the Union. That was a common charge upon the townships from which they could not claim im— munity. It might be that a certain township contributed .42300 or £4OO to the funds of the Union and yet only £5O of it might be spent on paupers from that town- ship. Mr. BALL said it would take a very small sum to maintain the paupers in his township. He would be glad to pay it instead of cautributing to the puor rate. 1 The CLERK : But that is not the law. Te estimates were then approved of, and the resolu- tion passed. "A HAPPY SUGGESTION !" THAT HOPE DEFERRED MAKETH THE lIKART SICK is just as true now as ever it was will be attested by all whose most cherished aspirations have remained unfulfilled. In every walk of life we encounter this hankering after the (supposed) unattainable, whilst in many cases the remedy is close at hand if those interested only knew how to avail themselves of it. It affects most businesses, the furnishing trade especially. For instance, a young man meets a maiden fair whose appearance and merits he approves. She, likewise, appreciates his qualities, and quickly an affection springs up between them. How pleasant they think it would be to marry and start hotssekeeping together. Then the stumbling block presents ittelf--where Is the cash to purchase furniture to come from ? With him, time past, like with most young fellows, "enough for the day has been the evil thereof." He has save I practically nothing so the marriage is postponed indefinitely. Now, this is where PITTS S step in with a timely suggestion. Instead of deferring the hope and making the hearts sick why not, by a fair and equitable arrangement, defer the payments and make both hearts glad? There are many other distinguished .scotch golfers besides those I have mentioned, but Mr Maxwell is regarded by Englishmen as a most doughty opponent and one of the toughest customers, North of the Tweed." What about your champions South of it Haven't you some great proficients at Hoyla.ke? " Well, yes we have. At the risk of myself being twitted with tall talk I would venture to back four of our Hoylake amateurs against any other four in the world." A Warrington Man's Novel Lighting Idea. Henry Ellison, greengrocer, of Golden-grove, Warrington, evidently considers that he has a mis- sion in life—viz., to demonstrate'to the powers that be that a light is a light, even though it may not be inside a lamp. At St. Helens Police Court, on Nionlay, Police Constable Peters, stated that on Saturday night, the Ist inst., he found Ellison sell- ing greengroceries in Peckers Hill-road. He had no light on the front of his cart, but was engaged at the back of the cart weighing goods by the light of a candle, which was placed inside a glass bottle. Ellison had knocked the bottom out of the bottle and turned it upside down, fixing the candle inside the bottle neck. Ellison.who was fined in July last for a similar offance, was now fined 5s and 4s 6d costs.
